title: Boil water to make it safe to drink
summary: Boiling is the most reliable way to kill the bacteria, viruses and protozoa in water when you have heat to spare. It is purification, not filtration: it kills things, it does not remove them.

steps.text: If the water is cloudy, let it settle, then pour the clear water off the top through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter. Boiling cloudy water works, but sediment shields some organisms and the result tastes bad enough that people avoid drinking it.
Bring the clear water to a rolling boil — a boil you cannot stir flat — and hold it there for one full minute. Time it. People consistently under-boil when guessing.
Above 6,500 feet of elevation, hold the rolling boil for three minutes instead of one. Water boils cooler at altitude, so it needs longer.
steps.caution: If you do not know your elevation, use three minutes. The cost is fuel. The cost of guessing low is illness.

steps.text: Let the water cool on its own. Do not add ice or cold untreated water to speed it up — that re-contaminates everything you just treated.
Store it in clean, covered containers. Boiled water tastes flat because the dissolved air has gone; pouring it between two clean containers a few times puts the air back.

failureModes.symptom: People get sick anyway
failureModes.cause: Treated water poured into a dirty container, or a container lid handled with unwashed hands
failureModes.remedy: Sanitise storage containers before use and treat the lid and pour spout as part of the container.

failureModes.symptom: Water still tastes and smells wrong after boiling
failureModes.cause: Chemical contamination, which boiling does not address and can concentrate
failureModes.remedy: Stop using that source. Boiling is the wrong tool for a chemical problem.

failureModes.symptom: Fuel runs out partway through the outage
failureModes.cause: Boiling is fuel-expensive and is usually budgeted optimistically
failureModes.remedy: Hold chemical treatment in reserve for when fuel runs low and keep boiling for the water you will drink soonest.

doesNotDo: Does not remove chemical contamination — pesticides, fuel, solvents, industrial runoff. Boiling evaporates water and can leave these MORE concentrated than before.
Does not remove heavy metals such as lead. Same concentration problem.
Does not remove salt. Boiling seawater and drinking the result will hurt you.
Does not remove sediment, cloudiness or bad taste. It kills organisms; it removes nothing.
Does not protect water after treatment. Boiled water put into a dirty bottle is dirty water.

title: Disinfect water with unscented household bleach
summary: Chemical disinfection when you have no fuel to boil. Cheap, light, and effective against most organisms — but the product matters, the dose matters, and the contact time matters.

steps.text: Check the label. You need sodium hypochlorite between 5% and 9%, with nothing else in it.
steps.caution: Do NOT use scented, colour-safe, splash-less, gel, or cleaner-added bleach. These contain additives that are not safe to drink and no amount of waiting makes them safe.

steps.text: If the water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth until it runs clear. Chlorine is consumed by the organic matter in cloudy water, so a dose that would work on clear water will fall short.
For 6% bleach, add 8 drops — about one-eighth of a teaspoon — per gallon of clear water. For 8.25% bleach, use 6 drops per gallon. Double the dose if the water is still cloudy after filtering.
Stir it and let it stand for 30 minutes. Contact time is doing the work; cutting it short is the most common mistake.
Smell it. It should smell faintly of chlorine. If it does not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes before drinking.
steps.caution: If it still does not smell of chlorine after a second dose, discard it and find another source. Bleach loses potency with age and yours may be dead.

failureModes.symptom: No chlorine smell after two doses
failureModes.cause: Bleach older than about a year, or stored hot, has lost most of its free chlorine
failureModes.remedy: Replace stored bleach annually and write the date on the bottle. Treat an old bottle as cleaning supply, not water treatment.

failureModes.symptom: Illness despite treatment
failureModes.cause: Dosed cloudy water without filtering first, or did not wait the full contact time
failureModes.remedy: Filter to clear, then dose, then wait by the clock rather than by feel.

failureModes.symptom: Water tastes strongly of chlorine
failureModes.cause: Overdose
failureModes.remedy: Let it stand uncovered for a few hours, or pour it between clean containers. Mild overdose is far safer than underdose.

doesNotDo: Does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Chlorine is poor against it; boiling or a filter rated for protozoa is required where Crypto is a risk.
Is less effective against Giardia than against bacteria and viruses, and needs the full contact time to work at all.
Does not remove chemical contamination, heavy metals, or salt.
Does not remove sediment or cloudiness — you must filter first, and the filtering is for the chlorine's benefit, not the taste.
Does not work with scented, splash-less, gel or cleaner-added bleach. Those are not water treatment products in any dose.

title: Choose and use a hollow-fibre water filter
summary: A 0.1-micron hollow-fibre filter removes bacteria and protozoa by physically straining them out. It is filtration, not purification. Most of these filters do not remove viruses, and that distinction is the whole reason to read this page.

steps.text: Check the rating. You want 0.1 micron absolute — not nominal. A nominal rating is an average pore size, which means some pores are larger and some organisms get through.
Pre-filter cloudy water through a cloth. Silt clogs hollow fibres quickly and a clogged filter is a dead filter.
Keep the clean side clean. Never let untreated water touch the output nozzle, and never put the output into a bottle that held untreated water.
steps.caution: Cross-contamination at the output is the most common way people get sick while using a perfectly good filter.

steps.text: Backflush according to the manufacturer's direction when flow slows. Flow rate is the only warning you get that the filter is loading up.

Protect it from freezing. Water trapped in the fibres expands when it freezes and cracks them — and a cracked hollow-fibre filter looks exactly like a working one while passing everything straight through.
steps.caution: A filter that has frozen while wet must be discarded. There is no field test that will tell you whether it is still intact.

steps.text: Where viruses are a credible risk — sewage contamination, flood water, dense human activity upstream — follow filtration with chemical treatment or boiling. The filter handles the sediment and protozoa; the second step handles the viruses.

failureModes.symptom: Flow slows to nothing
failureModes.cause: Silt loading from unfiltered source water
failureModes.remedy: Backflush. Pre-filter through cloth in future.

failureModes.symptom: Illness after use
failureModes.cause: Either viral contamination the filter was never rated for, or cross-contamination at the output
failureModes.remedy: Add a purification step and keep the output nozzle physically separated from untreated water.

failureModes.symptom: Filter passes water suspiciously fast after a cold night
failureModes.cause: Freeze damage has cracked the fibres
failureModes.remedy: Discard it. Do not attempt to assess it visually.

doesNotDo: Does NOT remove viruses. Viruses are roughly 0.02 to 0.3 micron and pass straight through a 0.1-micron filter. This is the single most important limitation of this tool.
Does not remove chemical contamination, pesticides, fuel or solvents.
Does not remove heavy metals such as lead or arsenic.
Does not remove salt.
Does not give any warning when it has failed. A freeze-cracked filter produces clear, fast-flowing, contaminated water.

title: Improvised sand and charcoal filtration column
summary: A layered sand and charcoal column clears muddy water and improves its taste. Read the next section before you read the steps: this does not make water safe to drink, and the popular belief that it does has killed people.

steps.text: Understand what you are building. This is a pre-treatment stage that makes water clear enough for boiling or chemical disinfection to work properly. It is a step before purification, never a substitute for it.
steps.caution: Water that comes out of this column is not drinkable. It is water that is now ready to be purified.

steps.text: Take a container and make drainage holes in the base. A bucket, a large bottle cut off at the bottom, or a cloth bag all work.

Lay a cloth across the bottom to stop the media washing out, then build upward: coarse gravel, then fine gravel, then coarse sand, then fine sand, then crushed charcoal from a wood fire, then another cloth layer on top to stop the inflow digging a channel.
Use charcoal from untreated wood only. Charcoal briquettes contain binders, accelerants and sometimes lighter fluid residue.
steps.caution: Never use briquettes or any treated or painted wood. You will add contamination rather than remove it.

steps.text: Rinse the column with several litres of water and discard every drop of it. New media sheds dust and fines for a long time.
Pour water in slowly so it percolates rather than channels. Fast water finds a path through and touches almost none of the media.
Now boil the output for one minute, or treat it chemically for 30 minutes. This is not an optional final step. It is the step that makes the water safe.

failureModes.symptom: Output is still cloudy
failureModes.cause: Channelling from pouring too fast, or media too coarse
failureModes.remedy: Add a finer sand layer and pour slowly onto a cloth or stone spreader.

failureModes.symptom: Output tastes of ash
failureModes.cause: Charcoal fines not rinsed out
failureModes.remedy: Keep rinsing and discarding until it runs clean.

failureModes.symptom: Someone drinks the output untreated and becomes ill
failureModes.cause: The widespread and incorrect belief that this is a water purifier
failureModes.remedy: Label the output container. Treat this as a hard rule in a group, not a preference.

doesNotDo: Does NOT make water microbiologically safe. It does not reliably remove bacteria, viruses or protozoa. Water from this column must still be boiled or chemically treated.

Does not remove chemical contamination, heavy metals or salt. The charcoal layer adsorbs some organic compounds and improves taste, but this is not activated carbon and it is not a treatment you can rely on.
Does not sterilise anything. Nothing in the column kills organisms.
Does not have any indicator of failure. Clear, pleasant-tasting water from this column can carry a full pathogen load.

title: Build and run a twin-bucket emergency toilet
summary: When the water stops, the toilet stops. Sanitation failure causes more illness in prolonged outages than any other single factor, and it is also the problem households plan for least. Two buckets and a bag of sawdust solve it.

steps.text: Stop flushing immediately if the water supply or the sewer is compromised. A toilet that will not drain, or a sewer backing up, turns the bathroom into the worst room in the house within a day.

Set up two buckets and keep them separate: one for urine, one for solids. Separating the two cuts odour dramatically and roughly halves the volume of waste you must store, because urine is the bulk and solids are the hazard.
Line the solids bucket with a heavy bag and put a two-inch layer of cover material in the bottom — sawdust, wood shavings, peat or dry soil.

After each use of the solids bucket, add enough cover material to hide the surface completely. Covered waste does not smell and does not attract flies. Flies are the mechanism by which this becomes everybody's problem.
Urine is nearly sterile when it leaves a healthy person and can be diluted and poured outside well away from any water source, garden bed or well head.
Seal each full solids bag, double-bag it, and store it in a covered container outside and away from where people walk and children play. Do not bury it near a well or a watercourse.
steps.caution: Do not burn it, and do not compost it in an ordinary garden compost heap. Neither reaches a temperature that reliably kills pathogens.

steps.text: Put soap, water and hand sanitiser immediately next to the buckets, not across the room. Hand hygiene at the point of use is what actually breaks the transmission chain, and distance is the reason people skip it.

failureModes.symptom: Strong smell within a day
failureModes.cause: Not enough cover material, or urine and solids mixed
failureModes.remedy: Separate the streams and cover more generously. If you can see the surface, you have not used enough.

failureModes.symptom: Flies
failureModes.cause: Uncovered waste, or a bucket left open between uses
failureModes.remedy: Cover after every use and keep a lid on between uses.

failureModes.symptom: Household gastrointestinal illness spreading
failureModes.cause: Hand hygiene failure, almost always
failureModes.remedy: Move hand-washing supplies to arm's reach of the bucket and make it the household's one non-negotiable rule.

failureModes.symptom: Cover material runs out on day four
failureModes.cause: Everyone underestimates the quantity
failureModes.remedy: Budget roughly a gallon of cover material per person per week and store more than you think you need. It is cheap and it is the whole system.

doesNotDo: Does not treat or sterilise waste. It contains and covers it. The bags remain hazardous until properly disposed of.
Does not make the waste safe to compost in a normal garden heap, or safe to burn.
Does not substitute for hand hygiene. The buckets reduce exposure; soap and water break transmission.
Does not solve greywater — washing and cooking water still needs somewhere to go.
Does not work indefinitely. It buys weeks, not months, and the limit is storage space for sealed bags.

title: Making decisions when you are frightened and tired
summary: Stress does predictable things to judgement: it narrows attention, biases you toward whatever you did last time, and makes doing nothing feel like a decision. Knowing the failure modes in advance is most of the defence.

steps.text: Decide the big things before you are frightened. Evacuation triggers, rally points and who collects which child are decisions to make on an ordinary Tuesday. Written down, they survive a bad night; held in your head, they do not.

Watch for tunnelling. Under stress people fixate on one problem — usually the loudest or most recent — and stop noticing the others. Deliberately widen your view every so often: water, warmth, people, exit.

Treat 'wait and see' as a choice, not a pause. It is sometimes correct. It is also what people do when a decision is uncomfortable, and the two feel identical from the inside. Say out loud what you are waiting FOR and what you will do when you see it.

Eat, drink and sleep on purpose. Low blood sugar and sleep debt degrade judgement faster and earlier than almost anyone estimates, and the first thing to go is the ability to notice that your judgement has degraded.
Give one person the decision at any moment, especially in a group. Shared responsibility reliably produces no decision at all. Rotate it when that person is tired.
Write down what you decide and when. Memory under stress is unreliable, and in a multi-day event you will genuinely not remember whether you turned the gas off.

failureModes.symptom: Hours pass with nothing decided
failureModes.cause: Diffused responsibility in a group, or waiting for information that is not coming
failureModes.remedy: Name a decision-maker and a deadline. An adequate decision on time beats a good one too late.

failureModes.symptom: Fixating on one task while something important goes unattended
failureModes.cause: Attentional tunnelling, a normal stress response
failureModes.remedy: Set a recurring check: water, warmth, people, exit. Out loud, on a timer.

failureModes.symptom: Arguments escalating out of proportion
failureModes.cause: Sleep debt, hunger and uncertainty, not the thing being argued about
failureModes.remedy: Feed everyone and reconvene. Name the real cause; it defuses most of it.

doesNotDo: Does not make you calm. The physiological stress response happens regardless of preparation; the aim is to function while it is happening, not to avoid it.
Does not substitute for a written plan. These are habits that help you execute a plan, not a replacement for having one.
Does not address clinical anxiety, PTSD or acute psychological crisis, which are outside the scope of this library and need professional care.
Does not make group conflict go away. It reduces the conflict caused by exhaustion, which is most of it but not all of it.

title: Store water before you need it
summary: Stored water is the cheapest preparedness there is and the one most households skip. One gallon per person per day, in containers that will not fail, rotated before anyone has to think about it.

steps.text: Plan one gallon per person per day. That is the federal figure and it covers drinking and minimal hygiene — not bathing, not laundry, not flushing. Add more for hot climates, pregnancy, illness and anyone nursing.
Count pets. A medium dog drinks roughly a half to one gallon a day. Households that plan carefully for people still forget the animals.
Buy commercially bottled water if you can. It is sealed, dated and someone else's quality-control problem. Keep it in the original sealed container and respect the date on it.

If you fill your own, use food-grade containers only. Sanitise each one with a teaspoon of unscented bleach in a quart of water, swirl it over every interior surface, rinse, then fill from a safe tap.
steps.caution: Never reuse milk jugs or fruit-juice bottles. Milk protein and fruit sugars cannot be fully washed out and will grow bacteria. Milk jug plastic also degrades and splits.

steps.text: Label every container with the date you filled it and replace self-filled water every six months. Write it on the container, not in your phone.
Store away from sunlight, away from heat, and off bare concrete — concrete can leach into plastic over time and will transmit floor heat. A cool interior cupboard beats a garage.
Split the storage across at least two locations. One burst container or one inaccessible room should not take out your entire supply.

failureModes.symptom: Container splits and floods the storage area
failureModes.cause: Reused milk jugs, or a stack taller than the bottom container can carry
failureModes.remedy: Food-grade containers only, and stack no more than two high unless the container is rated for it.

failureModes.symptom: Water tastes stale or plastic
failureModes.cause: Dissolved air lost in storage, or heat and sunlight
failureModes.remedy: Pour between two clean containers to re-aerate. Move the store somewhere cool and dark.

failureModes.symptom: Six months pass and nobody rotates it
failureModes.cause: The date lives in somebody's head
failureModes.remedy: Write the date on the container and let the app's rotation queue surface it.

doesNotDo: Storing water does not purify it. Water that was unsafe when you bottled it is unsafe six months later.
A sealed container does not sterilise its contents. Sanitising the container before filling is a separate step and it matters.
Stored water does not cover sanitation. Flushing a toilet uses more water in one flush than a person drinks in a day, which is why the bucket toilet exists.
A date on commercial bottled water is a quality date, not a safety cliff — but it is also not an invitation to ignore rotation entirely.

title: Find the water already inside your house
summary: A typical house holds thirty to fifty gallons of drinkable water in the water heater alone, plus more in the pipes and the toilet tanks. Most people never find it because they do not know it is there and do not know how to get it out.

steps.text: Shut the incoming water off first, at the main. If the supply is contaminated, every minute it stays open is more contaminated water entering your tank and pipes.
Turn the water heater OFF before you draw from it. Gas to pilot or off; electric breaker off.
steps.caution: An electric element that fires in an empty or partly empty tank will burn out, and a gas heater left on can damage the tank. Turn it off and leave it off until the supply is restored and the tank is refilled.

steps.text: Open a hot tap somewhere high in the house. This lets air in; without it the tank will barely trickle.
Attach a hose to the drain valve at the base of the heater, or hold a container under it, and open the valve. Expect sediment in the first flow — let it settle and pour the clear water off.
Drain the pipes separately: open the highest faucet in the house to admit air, then collect from the lowest.
Toilet TANK water — the cistern on the back, not the bowl — is usable if nobody has put a chemical cleaner, dye or 'bloo' tablet in it. Treat it before drinking.
steps.caution: The bowl is never a drinking source, treated or not. Neither is a waterbed: the vinyl is treated with algaecides and plasticisers that are not safe to drink.

steps.text: Do not forget the ice in the freezer, and any water already in jugs, kettles and a filled bath.
Treat everything you recover unless it came from a sealed container. Boil for one minute, or use the chemical method. Recovering water and purifying it are two separate jobs.

failureModes.symptom: Almost nothing comes out of the heater
failureModes.cause: No air admitted
failureModes.remedy: Open a hot tap on an upper floor and try again.

failureModes.symptom: Water is rusty or full of grit
failureModes.cause: Years of sediment at the bottom of the tank
failureModes.remedy: Let it settle, decant the clear water, then filter and treat. Flushing the heater annually prevents this.

failureModes.symptom: Heater damaged when power returned
failureModes.cause: Left switched on while empty
failureModes.remedy: Breaker off before draining, and back on only after the tank is full again.

doesNotDo: Recovering this water does not make it safe. It still needs boiling or chemical treatment unless it came from a sealed bottle.
It does not help if the contamination arrived through the mains before you shut the valve — which is why shutting off first is step one, not step eight.
The toilet bowl is not a source. Neither is a waterbed, a swimming pool, or a hot tub: pool and spa water carries chemical treatment loads that boiling concentrates rather than removes.
Draining the heater does not refill it. Until mains supply returns you have taken a one-time withdrawal.

title: What a boil-water notice actually requires
summary: A boil-water notice means your utility cannot currently guarantee the water is free of organisms. It is the most common water emergency in the country by a wide margin, and most households under one are still brushing their teeth from the tap.

steps.text: Read which kind of notice it is. A boil-water notice is about microorganisms. A 'do not drink' or chemical advisory is a different thing entirely and boiling makes it worse, not better.
steps.caution: If the advisory names a chemical, do not boil. Boiling concentrates chemical contamination. Use bottled water until the utility says otherwise.

steps.text: For a boil notice: bring water to a rolling boil for one minute, three minutes above 6,500 feet. Then cool it and store it covered.
Apply it to everything that reaches a mouth. Drinking, ice, brushing teeth, washing produce, making formula, mixing juice, and the pet's bowl.
Throw out ice made during the notice period, and run the icemaker through a discard cycle after it lifts.

For dishes: wash in hot soapy water, then sanitise in a solution of one teaspoon of unscented bleach per gallon of water for at least a minute, and air-dry. A dishwasher with a sanitising cycle and a hot final rinse is also acceptable.
Showering and bathing are generally acceptable for healthy adults, but do not swallow the water. Supervise children, who will. Sponge-bathe infants rather than bathing them.
When the notice lifts, flush your household plumbing: run every cold tap for several minutes, replace water filter cartridges, and drain and refill the water heater if the utility advises it.

failureModes.symptom: Someone in the household is ill anyway
failureModes.cause: Toothbrushing, ice from before the notice, or the pet bowl
failureModes.remedy: Put a sign on the kitchen tap. Treating this as a household rule rather than an individual choice is what makes it work.

failureModes.symptom: Advisory lifted and the water still tastes wrong
failureModes.cause: Plumbing not flushed, old filter cartridge still in place
failureModes.remedy: Flush all taps and change filters.

failureModes.symptom: Boiling was applied to a chemical advisory
failureModes.cause: The two notices get confused constantly
failureModes.remedy: Read the notice. If it names a chemical, boiling is the wrong tool and increases the dose.

doesNotDo: Boiling does NOT address chemical contamination. If the advisory names a chemical, boiling concentrates it. This is the single most dangerous confusion in household water safety.
A boil notice does not mean the water is definitely contaminated — it means the utility cannot currently prove it is not. Treat it as real anyway.
Boiling does not clean the container you pour it into, the lid, or your hands.
A household filter pitcher is not a substitute for boiling during a notice. Most are designed for taste and chlorine, not for microbiology.

title: Getting water from snow and ice
summary: Snow looks like free water and is the most expensive water there is: eating it costs you body heat you may not be able to spare, and it is not clean. Melt it, treat it, and drink it warm.

steps.text: Do not eat snow. Melting it inside your body costs a great deal of heat at exactly the moment you need it, and in cold conditions that is how mild hypothermia becomes serious hypothermia.
steps.caution: This is the single most common winter mistake. Someone who is already cold and eats snow for thirst gets colder and dehydrates faster.

steps.text: Collect from a clean undisturbed area, away from roads, paths, animal tracks and anything downwind of a road. Grey or pink snow is not clean snow.
Start the pot with a little liquid water if you have any. A pot of dry snow over direct heat will scorch and give the whole batch a burnt taste before it melts.
Add snow gradually and keep the pot wet. Expect a poor yield — fresh powder is mostly air, and ten pots of snow make about one pot of water. Old compacted snow and ice yield far more per pot of fuel.
Prefer ice to snow when you have the choice. It melts with less fuel for the same volume of water.
Treat the melt the same as any surface water: bring it to a rolling boil for one minute, three above 6,500 feet. Snow is not distilled and falls through whatever is in the air.
Drink it warm rather than cold. Warm fluids help maintain core temperature; cold fluids work against it.

failureModes.symptom: Whole batch tastes burnt
failureModes.cause: Dry snow scorched on a hot pot base
failureModes.remedy: Always keep a little water in the pot and add snow to it.

failureModes.symptom: Fuel runs out far faster than expected
failureModes.cause: Melting snow is fuel-expensive and is almost always underestimated
failureModes.remedy: Budget fuel for melting separately from fuel for cooking, and gather ice rather than powder where possible.

failureModes.symptom: Someone gets colder while drinking plenty
failureModes.cause: Eating snow or drinking the melt cold
failureModes.remedy: Melt it, warm it, and never eat snow for thirst.

doesNotDo: Melting snow does not purify it. Snow is not sterile and is not distilled — it forms around airborne particles and collects whatever it falls through.
Does not remove chemical contamination, road salt, or anything deposited from traffic or industry.
Does not help with hydration if eaten frozen. It costs more body heat than it returns.
Freshly fallen snow being 'clean looking' does not make it safe. Clear and pleasant does not mean treated.
Does not apply to sea ice without care: new sea ice is salty and drinking it will dehydrate you faster than drinking nothing.

title: Collecting rainwater you can actually use
summary: Rain is the easiest volume of water to collect and the easiest to collect badly. The rain is reasonably clean; your roof is not.

steps.text: Check your state and local rules first. Rainwater collection is encouraged in some jurisdictions, restricted in others, and the restrictions are usually about volume and water rights rather than safety.

Know your roof. Asphalt shingle sheds granules and petroleum compounds. Treated wood shakes shed preservative. Older painted or flashed roofs may shed lead. Metal and tile are the cleanest common surfaces.
steps.caution: Do not collect drinking water from a roof with lead flashing, lead-based paint, or asbestos cement sheet. For those, collect for flushing and washing only.

steps.text: Divert the first flush. The first several gallons carry the accumulated bird droppings, dust, pollen and debris from the whole dry period. A simple standpipe that fills before flow reaches the barrel will do it.
Screen the inlet. A fine mesh keeps out leaves, insects and — critically — mosquitoes, which will breed in an open barrel within days.
Use an opaque, covered, food-grade container. Light grows algae; an open container is a drowning risk for small children and an invitation to everything else.
Let the collected water settle, draw from above the sediment, filter for clarity, then purify — boil for one minute or treat chemically. Clearing it and making it safe are two different operations.
Label the barrel plainly as untreated. In a household under stress, an unlabelled barrel of clear water will be drunk.

failureModes.symptom: Water smells and grows green
failureModes.cause: Light reaching the container
failureModes.remedy: Opaque container, sealed lid, screened inlet.

failureModes.symptom: Mosquito larvae in the barrel
failureModes.cause: Unscreened opening
failureModes.remedy: Fine mesh on every opening including the overflow.

failureModes.symptom: Persistent grit and a chemical taste
failureModes.cause: Asphalt shingle roof shedding granules and compounds
failureModes.remedy: Use this supply for flushing and washing, and find another source for drinking.

doesNotDo: Collecting rainwater does not purify it. Roof runoff carries bird and rodent droppings, which means it carries the organisms in them.
A first-flush diverter does not make the rest safe. It removes the worst of the debris; it removes no pathogens.
Does not remove what your roofing material contributes — lead, asbestos fibres, wood preservative or asphalt compounds are not removed by filtering or boiling.
Does not remove chemical contamination from the air in an industrial or wildfire-smoke area.
A screened, covered barrel does not stop the water going stale. Rotate it or use it for non-drinking purposes.

title: What your kitchen filter pitcher is for
summary: The filter jug in the fridge and the cartridge on the tap are taste-and-odour devices. In an emergency people reach for them first because they are already there, and they are close to useless for the thing that will actually make someone ill.

steps.text: Read what the filter is certified for. A carbon pitcher is usually certified for chlorine taste and odour, and sometimes for lead. That is a different certification from microbiological purification.
Treat any filter without an explicit microbiological claim as a taste device. If the box does not claim to remove bacteria, protozoa or viruses, it does not.
During a boil notice, boil first and filter afterwards if you want the taste improved. Filtering first and skipping the boil is the dangerous order.
Replace the cartridge on schedule, and replace it after any period when it filtered questionable water. A loaded carbon cartridge is a warm, wet, nutrient-rich place and will grow things.
steps.caution: A cartridge that has sat wet and unused for weeks is worse than no filter at all. Discard it rather than resuming use.

steps.text: Keep a filter that does make a microbiological claim — a 0.1-micron hollow-fibre or equivalent — as your actual emergency filter, and keep it separate from the kitchen jug so the two never get confused.

failureModes.symptom: Household falls ill despite 'filtering' everything
failureModes.cause: A taste filter used as a purifier
failureModes.remedy: Boil or chemically treat. Use the pitcher for taste afterwards.

failureModes.symptom: Filtered water tastes worse than the tap
failureModes.cause: Exhausted or colonised cartridge
failureModes.remedy: Replace it. Do not try to clean or dry it out for reuse.

doesNotDo: A carbon pitcher filter does NOT remove bacteria, protozoa or viruses unless it explicitly claims to. Almost none do.
It does not purify, sterilise or disinfect. It improves taste and odour and sometimes reduces specific chemicals it is certified for.
It does not make boil-notice water safe, and using it that way is the most likely way for a prepared household to still get sick.
It does not protect itself: a wet cartridge left unused becomes a culture medium.
A refrigerator door filter is the same device in a different housing and carries the same limits.

title: What to keep and what to throw out after an outage
summary: The fridge holds about four hours. A full freezer holds about forty-eight. Everything that follows is arithmetic from those two numbers, and the one rule that overrides all of it is that you never taste food to find out.

steps.text: Keep both doors shut. A closed refrigerator holds safe temperature for about four hours; a full freezer for about forty-eight, or about twenty-four if it is half full. Every opening spends that budget.
Fill the empty space in the freezer now, before you need it. Containers of water frozen solid make a half-empty freezer behave like a full one and give you drinking water afterwards.
Put a thermometer in the fridge and one in the freezer. Guessing by touch is how people get this wrong, and an appliance thermometer costs very little.
When power returns, read the thermometers before you open anything else. Frozen food at 40°F or below, or still holding ice crystals, is safe and may be refrozen — though the texture will suffer.
Discard any perishable — meat, poultry, fish, eggs, soft cheese, cut fruit, leftovers — that has been above 40°F for four hours or more.
steps.caution: Discard it unopened and untasted. Some of the organisms that cause serious illness produce no smell, no taste and no visible change.

steps.text: Discard anything that came into contact with floodwater, including sealed packaging that is not fully waterproof. Screw-top jars, crimped caps and cardboard are not waterproof.
Work through the food in order: fridge first, then freezer, then the shelf-stable store. The shelf-stable store is the one that will still be there next week.

failureModes.symptom: Food looked and smelled fine and someone got ill
failureModes.cause: Pathogenic organisms frequently produce no sensory change at all
failureModes.remedy: Use the clock and the thermometer, not your nose. This is why the rule is absolute.

failureModes.symptom: Freezer thawed far sooner than expected
failureModes.cause: Half-empty freezer, or the door opened repeatedly to check
failureModes.remedy: Keep it full with water containers and resist opening it.

failureModes.symptom: Refrozen food is mushy and unpleasant
failureModes.cause: Ice crystals rupturing cell walls on the first thaw
failureModes.remedy: Normal and not a safety problem. Use it in cooked dishes rather than served plain.

doesNotDo: Smelling or tasting food does NOT tell you whether it is safe. Several of the organisms that cause serious illness produce no odour, no off taste and no visible change.
Refreezing does not restore quality, and it does not make unsafe food safe — it only preserves food that was still safe when you refroze it.
A full freezer does not hold for 48 hours if the door is opened. The figure assumes it stays shut.
Cooking does not reliably rescue food that has been warm for hours. Some bacterial toxins are heat-stable and survive cooking even when the bacteria do not.
These timings do not apply to food that touched floodwater, regardless of temperature.

title: Build a food store you will actually eat
summary: The most common food-storage mistake is buying a pallet of something nobody in the house likes and discovering that fact during the emergency. Store what you already eat, store more of it, and eat it in order.

steps.text: Start from your own shopping list, not from a survival list. Buy two of what you already buy one of, and you have a rotating store within a month without a single unfamiliar item.
Budget around 2,000 calories per adult per day as a planning figure, more for physical work or cold. Children eat less by weight and more by appetite than people expect.
Weight the first week toward food that needs no cooking and no water: canned goods with pull tabs, nut butters, crackers, dried fruit, tinned fish, shelf-stable milk.

Add bulk staples — rice, beans, oats, pasta — only after the no-cook tier exists. They are by far the cheapest calories and they need both water and heat, so they are a second-line resource, not a first.
Store a manual can opener with the food, not in a drawer. More than one household has discovered their entire store was behind an electric opener.
Rotate by eating. Put new purchases at the back and cook from the front. A store you eat from never expires and never needs a special trip to replace.
Include comfort. Coffee, tea, sweets, something familiar for a child. Morale is a real logistical input over a week-long event and it costs almost nothing to plan for.

failureModes.symptom: Store expires untouched
failureModes.cause: Stocked with food the household does not normally eat
failureModes.remedy: Buy what you eat. The rotation problem solves itself.

failureModes.symptom: Plenty of calories, nobody will eat them
failureModes.cause: Monotony, or unfamiliar food during an already stressful week
failureModes.remedy: Variety and familiarity, and at least a few things people actually like.

failureModes.symptom: Cannot open the cans
failureModes.cause: Electric opener, or the manual one lives somewhere else
failureModes.remedy: A manual opener stored with the food, and a second one in the kit.

doesNotDo: A food store does not replace water. Dehydrated and bulk staples increase your water requirement rather than reducing it.
It does not feed you without a way to open it, and for staples, without heat and water.
Shelf-stable does not mean indefinite. Oils go rancid, cans corrode at the seam, and heat shortens everything.
A long-shelf-life bucket meal does not address dietary restrictions, allergies or medical diets, and the emergency is a bad time to discover that.

title: Cooking when the power is out
summary: Most of the people hurt cooking during an outage are not hurt by fire. They are poisoned by carbon monoxide from a device that was working exactly as designed, indoors, where it should never have been.

steps.text: Cook outdoors. Charcoal grills, camp stoves, gas grills and any fuel-burning cooker belong outside, away from doors, windows and vents.
steps.caution: Never burn charcoal indoors, in a garage, in a tent, on a balcony or in a vehicle. Charcoal produces lethal amounts of carbon monoxide and has killed people in rooms with windows open. A camp stove is not an indoor appliance either.

steps.text: A gas cooktop that lights with a match may still work when the electricity is out. The oven usually will not, because the electronic ignition and controls need power. Never use a gas oven or cooktop for heating the room.
Have a carbon monoxide alarm with working batteries, and know that it is a last defence rather than a permission slip.
Cook in order of perishability: fridge food first, then freezer, then shelf-stable. One cooking session that uses up several thawing items is better fuel economy than several small ones.
Keep a lid on the pot. It roughly halves the fuel needed to reach a boil, and fuel is the constraint.
Favour one-pot meals and foods that rehydrate rather than simmer. Soaking beans overnight in treated water and then boiling is far cheaper in fuel than boiling them from dry.
Have at least one meal plan that needs no heat at all, for the days when fuel has to be saved for water treatment.

failureModes.symptom: Headache, dizziness and nausea in several people at once
failureModes.cause: Carbon monoxide. It is odourless and the early symptoms read exactly like flu
failureModes.remedy: Get everyone outside into fresh air immediately and call emergency services. Do not re-enter to investigate.

failureModes.symptom: Fuel exhausted after two days
failureModes.cause: Boiling with the lid off, and cooking food that needs long simmering
failureModes.remedy: Lid on, one-pot meals, soak before boiling, and reserve fuel for water.

failureModes.symptom: Gas cooktop will not light
failureModes.cause: Electronic ignition needs power
failureModes.remedy: A match or lighter at the burner usually works on an older cooktop. Never do this with an oven.

doesNotDo: Opening a window does NOT make indoor charcoal or camp-stove use safe. This has killed people in ventilated rooms and is the central misunderstanding of this topic.
A carbon monoxide alarm does not make an unsafe practice safe. It tells you that you have already made a mistake.
A gas oven is never a room heater, and using it as one is a recognised cause of fatal poisoning.
Cooking does not make unsafe food safe — see what to keep and what to throw out after an outage.
A camp stove does not run indefinitely on one canister. Budget fuel for water treatment first and cooking second.

title: Rationing food, and why you should not ration water
summary: The instinct under scarcity is to stretch everything. For food that is often correct. For water it is wrong, and the official guidance says so plainly: drink what you need today and look for more tomorrow.

steps.text: Do not ration drinking water unless an authority instructs you to. Drink what your body needs today. A dehydrated person makes worse decisions, works less effectively and becomes a casualty rather than a help.
steps.caution: Rationing water to stretch a supply is a well-documented way to arrive at the end of the emergency both out of water and already dehydrated. Reduce the demand instead: reduce activity, stay cool, stay out of the sun.

steps.text: Reduce water demand rather than water intake. Rest in the coolest available place, work in the cooler parts of the day, and eat less salty food.
For food, know the real timescale. A healthy adult tolerates substantially reduced intake for days without danger. Thirst is urgent in hours; hunger is not.
Feed children, pregnant and nursing people, the ill and the elderly on their normal schedule. They have far less margin than a healthy adult and should not be rationed to match the group.
Eat the food that will spoil first, not the food you like least. Spoilage sets the order, not preference.
Eat less if water is short. Digestion, and protein digestion especially, costs water. If water is the binding constraint, a large meal makes it worse.
Decide the ration openly and as a household. Unexplained portion changes read as unfairness and cause more trouble than hunger does.

failureModes.symptom: People are dehydrated despite water remaining in store
failureModes.cause: Rationing water by instinct
failureModes.remedy: Drink to need. Cut demand, not intake.

failureModes.symptom: Arguments about portions
failureModes.cause: Rationing decided privately and applied silently
failureModes.remedy: Decide it in the open, state the reason, and apply it to the adults first.

failureModes.symptom: A child becomes unwell quickly
failureModes.cause: Children rationed on the same terms as adults
failureModes.remedy: Children, pregnant and nursing people, the ill and the elderly are not rationed.

doesNotDo: Rationing water does NOT extend your endurance. It brings forward the point at which you stop functioning, which is why the federal guidance says not to.
Eating less does not reduce your water requirement to zero — but eating more, especially protein, increases it.
Rationing does not apply to children, pregnant or nursing people, the ill or the elderly.
Going without food does not make you tougher. It makes you cold, slow and bad-tempered, and all three have consequences in an emergency.
This is general guidance for short-duration emergencies, not medical advice for anyone with diabetes or any condition requiring regular intake.

title: Home canning, and the one mistake that kills
summary: Home canning is genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous, and the danger concentrates in a single error: processing low-acid food in a boiling-water bath instead of a pressure canner. Botulinum spores survive boiling. The toxin they then produce is among the most lethal substances known.

steps.text: Separate your food into high-acid and low-acid before anything else. High-acid — most fruit, properly acidified pickles, jams — can be processed in a boiling-water bath. Low-acid — all vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, soups, and anything mixed — requires a pressure canner.
steps.caution: This single distinction is the whole safety story. A boiling-water bath cannot reach the temperature needed to destroy botulinum spores in low-acid food. No amount of extra boiling time substitutes for pressure.

steps.text: Use a tested, current recipe from a federal or extension source, and follow it exactly: the jar size, the headspace, the processing time and the pressure are all part of the safety margin, not suggestions.
Do not scale, substitute or improvise. Adding extra vegetables to a tested tomato recipe lowers its acidity and moves it out of the category the processing time was validated for.
Adjust processing for altitude. Water boils cooler and pressure canners read differently as elevation rises, and published tables give the correction.
Check every seal after cooling. A properly sealed lid is concave and does not flex. Refrigerate and eat anything that did not seal, rather than re-processing it.
Label every jar with contents and date, and use within a year for best quality.
Before eating any home-canned low-acid food, boil it for ten minutes — longer at altitude — as a final safeguard. Botulinum toxin, unlike the spores, is destroyed by heat.
Discard without tasting any jar that is bulging, leaking, spurting on opening, cracked, mouldy, discoloured, foamy, or that smells wrong.
steps.caution: Do not taste to check. Do not feed it to an animal to check. Dispose of it sealed, so no person or animal can reach it, and wash everything it touched.

failureModes.symptom: A jar spurts or foams on opening
failureModes.cause: Gas production from microbial growth
failureModes.remedy: Discard sealed and untasted. Clean every surface it contacted.

failureModes.symptom: Jar failed to seal
failureModes.cause: Chipped rim, debris on the rim, incorrect headspace, reused single-use lid
failureModes.remedy: Refrigerate and use within days. Do not re-process.

failureModes.symptom: Jars seal but spoil months later
failureModes.cause: Under-processing, or an untested recipe
failureModes.remedy: Return to a tested recipe and verify your pressure gauge annually.

doesNotDo: A boiling-water bath does NOT make low-acid food safe. Botulinum spores survive boiling, and this is the error that causes the deaths.
A good seal does NOT mean the contents are safe. Botulinum grows precisely in a sealed, oxygen-free jar, and it produces no bulge, no smell and no off taste in many cases.
Looking, smelling and tasting do not detect botulinum toxin. Tasting to check is how people are poisoned.
An electric multicooker is not a pressure canner unless it is specifically tested and labelled for canning. Most are not.
Home canning does not preserve nutritional content indefinitely, and it does not rescue produce that was already spoiling.

title: Feeding an infant in an emergency
summary: An infant has almost no margin. Dehydration that an adult would shrug off is an emergency in a baby, and the water used to make formula matters more than any other water in the household.

steps.text: If the infant is breastfed, continue. Breastfeeding during an emergency is the most reliable, safest and most portable option available, and stress does not stop milk production — though it can slow letdown, which rest and fluids help.
Ready-to-feed liquid formula is the safest option when formula is needed, because it requires no water and no mixing. Prioritise it in your store over powder for exactly this reason.
If using concentrate or powder, make it with safe water only — bottled, or water boiled for one minute and cooled. Powdered infant formula is not a sterile product.
steps.caution: Never dilute formula to stretch it. Over-diluted formula causes water intoxication and malnutrition, and it has killed infants. Make it exactly to the label.

steps.text: Prepare one feed at a time and discard what is not taken within an hour. Do not save a partly finished bottle for later.
Wash hands with soap and safe water before preparing any feed; use sanitiser only when soap and water are not available.
Clean bottles and teats with safe water and soap, then sanitise by boiling for five minutes if the water supply is in question.
Watch for dehydration: fewer than six wet nappies a day, no tears when crying, a dry mouth, unusual sleepiness, or a sunken soft spot. Any of these is a reason to seek medical help urgently.
steps.caution: Do not give an infant under one year plain water, juice, or home-made rehydration mixtures as a substitute for feeding. Seek medical care.

steps.text: Keep a written record of feeds when the household is disrupted. Under stress people genuinely lose track of when a baby last fed.

failureModes.symptom: Formula running low and feeds stretched
failureModes.cause: The instinct to ration
failureModes.remedy: Never dilute. Seek supply through emergency services, shelters or a pharmacy — formula is one of the first things relief operations distribute.

failureModes.symptom: Infant unsettled and feeding poorly after a disruption
failureModes.cause: Stress and routine disruption, affecting both infant and carer
failureModes.remedy: Quiet, warmth, skin contact, and rest and fluids for the feeding parent.

failureModes.symptom: No safe water for formula
failureModes.cause: Supply interrupted
failureModes.remedy: Ready-to-feed liquid formula needs none. This is why it belongs in the store.

doesNotDo: Diluting formula does NOT stretch it safely. It causes water intoxication and malnutrition and has killed infants.
Boiling water does not make powdered formula sterile — the powder itself is not a sterile product, which is why safe water and prompt use both matter.
Plain water, juice, cow's milk or a home-made rehydration mixture is not a substitute for formula or breast milk in an infant under one year.
This page does not cover illness in an infant. Vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or refusal to feed in a baby is a reason to reach a clinician, not to self-manage.
Hand sanitiser does not replace soap and water for preparing a feed when soap and water are available.

title: Eating for a week with no heat and no water to spare
summary: The first days of an outage are the ones where fuel is most uncertain and water most precious. A no-cook plan removes food from the list of things competing for both.

steps.text: Build the first three days entirely from food that needs no heat and no added water: tinned fish and meat, beans in their liquid, nut butters, crackers, oatcakes, dried fruit, nuts, shelf-stable milk, tinned fruit in juice.
Prefer pull-tab cans, and keep a manual opener anyway. Tabs break.
Use the liquid in the can. Bean and vegetable liquid is water you have already paid for and it is sterile until opened.
Front-load the fridge. The first day's eating should come out of the refrigerator, which is on the shortest clock.
Keep one meal per person per day that needs no preparation at all, for the hours when someone is too tired, too cold or too busy to assemble anything.
Plan for the washing up: a no-cook plan that generates a sink of greasy dishes has quietly spent the water it was supposed to save. Eat from packaging, and keep paper plates in the store.

failureModes.symptom: Water disappears faster than expected
failureModes.cause: Cooking and washing up, not drinking
failureModes.remedy: No-cook meals and disposable or wiped plates for the first days.

failureModes.symptom: Nobody wants to eat
failureModes.cause: Cold food, cold house, stress
failureModes.remedy: Keep one hot drink per person per day in the fuel budget. It does more for morale than a hot meal.

failureModes.symptom: The can opener is missing
failureModes.cause: It lives in a drawer, not in the store
failureModes.remedy: One stored with the food, one in the go bag.

doesNotDo: A no-cook plan does not meet long-term nutritional needs. It is a bridge over the first few days, not a diet.
It does not remove the need for water — it reduces it. People still drink.
It does not suit everyone: infants, people with dietary or medical restrictions, and anyone with chewing or swallowing difficulty need planning of their own.
Canned food is not indefinitely safe once opened. Without refrigeration, an opened can is a few hours of food, not a day's.

title: Bulk staples: the cheapest calories and their conditions
summary: Rice, beans, oats and pasta are the cheapest survival calories available by a very wide margin. They also arrive with conditions attached — water, heat and time — which is why they belong behind the no-cook tier rather than in front of it.

steps.text: Choose staples that store well: white rice, dried beans and lentils, rolled oats, pasta, salt, sugar, honey. Brown rice and wholegrain flour contain oil and go rancid in months rather than years.
Store in food-grade buckets with sealed lids, or in mylar bags inside buckets. The bucket keeps rodents out; the bag keeps air and light out.
Use oxygen absorbers sized to the container. They remove the oxygen that supports insect life and oxidation, and they are the difference between two years and twenty.
Freeze newly bought grain for several days before packing it if you can. It kills insect eggs that arrived with the grain, which is where pantry moth infestations actually come from.
Store cool, dark and dry, off bare concrete, and label every container with contents and date.
Budget the water. Dried beans need soaking and then an hour or more of boiling; rice needs roughly twice its volume in water. A staple store without a water store is a store of nothing.
Cook at least one meal from your bulk store before you depend on it. Beans in particular take far longer than people expect and some people's digestion needs a gradual introduction.

failureModes.symptom: Pantry moths throughout the store
failureModes.cause: Insect eggs present in the grain when it was packed
failureModes.remedy: Freeze new grain before packing, and use oxygen absorbers in sealed containers.

failureModes.symptom: Rancid, soapy-smelling grain
failureModes.cause: Wholegrain products stored too long, or stored warm
failureModes.remedy: Store white rice rather than brown for long terms, and keep the store cool.

failureModes.symptom: Beans will not soften however long they are boiled
failureModes.cause: Very old beans, or hard water
failureModes.remedy: Rotate the store. Old beans are a known and frustrating failure, and a pinch of baking soda in the soak helps.

doesNotDo: Bulk staples do NOT feed you without water and heat. They increase your water requirement substantially.
An oxygen absorber does not sterilise, does not kill adult insects reliably, and does not rescue grain that was already infested.
A sealed bucket is not rodent-proof if it is not actually sealed; rodents chew through thin plastic readily.
Staples alone are not adequate nutrition over weeks. They are calories, not a diet, and lack fat, vitamins and variety.
A twenty-year storage claim assumes cool, dark and dry. In a hot garage the real figure is a small fraction of that.

title: Heat one room, not a house
summary: A house without heating cannot be kept warm. A single room can. Choosing the room before you are cold, and committing to it, is most of the work.

steps.text: Pick the room now. Small, interior if possible, few windows, below the top floor, with a door you can close. A small room with four bodies in it stays markedly warmer than a large one.
Close the rest of the house. Shut doors to unused rooms and close their heating vents; put a rolled towel at the base of the door to the chosen room.

Deal with the windows. Close curtains and blinds at dusk, and open south-facing ones during daylight for solar gain. Plastic sheeting taped over the frame makes a real difference and so does a blanket hung over the curtain rail.
Get off the floor. Floors conduct heat away faster than air does. Mattresses, cushions, rugs and cardboard between people and the floor are worth more than another blanket on top.
Build a smaller volume inside the room. A blanket fort over a bed, or a tent pitched indoors, traps body heat in a space small enough for bodies to actually warm.
Sleep together where that is appropriate, and keep pets in the room. Shared body heat is the single largest heat source you have when the power is out.
Eat and drink warm. Digestion produces heat, and a hot drink raises both core temperature and morale for very little fuel.

failureModes.symptom: Room never gets warm despite everyone being in it
failureModes.cause: Too large a room, or heat draining through the floor and windows
failureModes.remedy: Move to a smaller room, insulate under people, cover the windows.

failureModes.symptom: People keep leaving the warm room
failureModes.cause: No light, nothing to do, no food in the room
failureModes.remedy: Move lighting, food, water and entertainment into the room so there is no reason to leave it.

failureModes.symptom: Condensation and damp bedding
failureModes.cause: Several people breathing in a sealed small room
failureModes.remedy: Ventilate briefly but regularly. Damp bedding insulates far worse than dry.

doesNotDo: Sealing a room does NOT make it safe to run a fuel-burning heater inside it. The better sealed the room, the faster carbon monoxide accumulates.
This does not keep a house from freezing. Pipes in the unheated part of the house are still at risk and may need draining.
It does not substitute for proper cold-weather clothing and bedding, and it does not help someone who is already hypothermic.
Candles are not a heat source. They are a significant fire risk and, in a sealed room, an oxygen consumer.

title: Heating without power, without poisoning anyone
summary: Every winter, people who survived the storm are killed by the thing they used to stay warm. Carbon monoxide is colourless, odourless, and its early symptoms are indistinguishable from being cold, tired and stressed — which everyone already is.

steps.text: Install carbon monoxide alarms on every sleeping level, with batteries you have actually tested, before any cold weather. This is the one item in this topic that belongs in the house year-round.
steps.caution: Carbon monoxide is odourless and colourless. You will not smell it, and the early symptoms — headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion — are exactly what a cold, tired, stressed person expects to feel anyway.

steps.text: Never burn charcoal indoors. Not in a fireplace, not in a garage, not on a balcony, not in a tent. Charcoal produces lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide and has killed people in rooms with windows open.
Never use a gas oven, gas cooktop or camp stove to heat a room. They are not designed for it and are not vented for it.
Never run a generator indoors, in a garage, in a crawlspace or in a porch, even with doors and windows open. Keep it outdoors and at least 20 feet from any door, window or vent.

Unvented fuel-burning heaters — kerosene, propane 'portable buddy' types — are legal in some places and not others and are only as safe as their ventilation and their oxygen-depletion sensor. If you use one, follow the manufacturer's clearances exactly, never run it while sleeping, and crack a window.
A wood stove or fireplace is fine if the flue is open, the chimney has been swept, and the fire is screened. A blocked or unswept flue puts the combustion products into the room.
Keep anything that burns at least three feet from anything that can catch — bedding, curtains, furniture, clothing left to dry.

If an alarm sounds, or several people have headache and nausea at once, get everyone outside into fresh air immediately and call emergency services from outside. Do not go back in to investigate or to open windows.
steps.caution: Do not re-enter the building. People die going back in.

failureModes.symptom: Several household members feel ill at the same time
failureModes.cause: Carbon monoxide. Simultaneous onset across several people is the signature
failureModes.remedy: Everyone outside now; call from outside; do not re-enter.

failureModes.symptom: Alarm sounds and is assumed faulty
failureModes.cause: Alarms are usually assumed to be wrong
failureModes.remedy: Treat every activation as real. Leave, then investigate from outside.

failureModes.symptom: Fire starts overnight
failureModes.cause: Heater too close to bedding, or a candle left burning
failureModes.remedy: Three feet of clearance, nothing burning while people sleep.

doesNotDo: Opening a window does NOT make indoor charcoal, generator or camp-stove use safe. This is the central and most lethal misunderstanding in winter preparedness.
A carbon monoxide alarm does not prevent poisoning. It warns you that it has already started, and only if its batteries are good.
An oxygen-depletion sensor on a portable heater does not detect carbon monoxide. It detects falling oxygen, which is a different thing and can lag behind a dangerous CO level.
Your nose does not detect carbon monoxide. There is nothing to smell.
Surviving a CO exposure does not mean you are fine. Delayed neurological effects are well documented, and anyone exposed should be assessed by a clinician.

title: Recognising and handling hypothermia
summary: Hypothermia does not announce itself. The person affected is the least able to notice it, because the first thing the cold takes is judgement — which is why somebody else has to be watching.

steps.text: Know the signs. Shivering, then slurred or mumbled speech, fumbling hands, stumbling, confusion, drowsiness and poor judgement. In infants, bright red cold skin and unusual stillness.
Treat shivering that STOPS as a worsening sign, not an improvement. As core temperature falls far enough the body stops shivering, and that is the point at which this becomes an emergency.
steps.caution: Severe hypothermia is a medical emergency. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

steps.text: Get the person out of the cold. If you cannot get indoors, shelter them from wind, and insulate them from the ground — the ground takes heat faster than the air does.
Remove wet clothing and replace it with dry coverings. Wet clothing against skin will keep cooling them however many blankets go on top.
Warm the core first, gently: warm dry compresses to the neck, chest and groin. Blankets, and shared body heat if that is what you have.
Do not rub or massage the arms and legs, and do not rewarm with a hot bath, a heat lamp or a direct heat source.
steps.caution: Rubbing the limbs and rapid external rewarming both drive cold blood from the extremities back toward the core and place additional strain on the heart. Warm the core, slowly.

steps.text: Give warm, sweet, non-alcoholic drinks only if the person is fully conscious and able to swallow. Never force fluids on someone who is not alert. Never give alcohol — it feels warming and accelerates heat loss.
Handle them gently and keep them horizontal. If there are no signs of life, begin CPR and continue while help is coming.

failureModes.symptom: Person insists they are fine and resists help
failureModes.cause: Impaired judgement is an early symptom, not stubbornness
failureModes.remedy: Do not take their assessment. Act on what you observe.

failureModes.symptom: Condition worsens after being brought inside and warmed
failureModes.cause: Rapid external rewarming or vigorous handling
failureModes.remedy: Warm the core gently and slowly. Keep them still and horizontal.

failureModes.symptom: Shivering stopped and was read as recovery
failureModes.cause: The most dangerous misreading in cold injury
failureModes.remedy: Treat cessation of shivering as deterioration and call for emergency help.

doesNotDo: Rubbing the arms and legs does NOT help and can make things worse by driving cold blood to the core.
A hot bath, heat lamp or direct heat does not safely rewarm a hypothermic person. Rapid external rewarming is dangerous.
Alcohol does not warm anyone. It dilates surface vessels, increases heat loss, and impairs the judgement that is already failing.
This page is not a substitute for emergency medical care, and nothing here treats severe hypothermia — it buys time until help arrives.
It does not cover frostbite, which is a different injury with different handling, or immersion in cold water.

title: Extreme heat with no air conditioning
summary: Heat kills more people in the United States in a typical year than any other weather hazard, and an outage during a heatwave removes the thing most households rely on entirely. It is also the hazard where a fan can make things worse.

steps.text: Drink before you are thirsty, and keep drinking. Thirst lags behind need in the heat, and in older adults it lags further.
Find the coolest part of the building — usually the lowest floor, interior, away from windows — and stay in it during the hottest hours.

Close windows, blinds and curtains during the day on the sunlit side, and open up at night if the outside air has actually dropped below the inside temperature. Check before you open; sometimes it has not.
Understand what a fan does. Moving air helps while sweat can still evaporate. Above roughly 95°F a fan blows hot air across you and can increase heat gain rather than relieve it.
steps.caution: Do not rely on a fan as your only cooling measure in very high temperatures. The CDC is explicit that fans are not protective in extreme heat.

steps.text: Wet skin, not just wet clothing. A damp cloth on the neck, wrists and ankles, a cool shower, or a basin of water for the feet moves real heat.
Leave if you can. A public cooling centre, a library, a shopping centre or a friend's house with power is a better answer than enduring it. This is the hazard where leaving is most often correct.
Check on neighbours, particularly older people living alone, people with chronic illness and anyone without transport. Heat deaths concentrate among people who were alone.
Know heat stroke: body temperature very high, hot skin, confusion, slurred speech, loss of consciousness, and sometimes no sweating at all. It is a medical emergency.
steps.caution: Call 911 immediately for suspected heat stroke, move the person to shade or indoors, and cool them aggressively with water and air movement while you wait. Do not give fluids to someone who is not fully conscious.

failureModes.symptom: Someone deteriorates despite drinking plenty
failureModes.cause: Heat stroke is a failure of thermoregulation, not simple dehydration
failureModes.remedy: Cool aggressively and call emergency services. Water alone will not fix it.

failureModes.symptom: House hotter at night than outside
failureModes.cause: Thermal mass holding the day's heat with windows shut
failureModes.remedy: Ventilate once outside air is genuinely cooler, and check rather than assume.

failureModes.symptom: An older relative is found unwell
failureModes.cause: Reduced thirst sensation, medications affecting heat regulation, and being alone
failureModes.remedy: Daily check-ins during any heat event. Put it in the plan.

doesNotDo: A fan does NOT protect you in extreme heat. Above roughly 95°F it can add heat rather than remove it, and treating it as sufficient is a documented cause of death.
Drinking water does not prevent or treat heat stroke. Heat stroke is a breakdown of temperature regulation and needs aggressive cooling and emergency care.
Salt tablets are not a recommended response and can cause harm.
This page does not cover heat illness in infants, who overheat far faster than adults, or anyone whose medication affects heat tolerance — ask a clinician in advance.
Alcohol and large amounts of caffeine do not help and contribute to fluid loss.

title: Sealing a room, and when it is the wrong answer
summary: Sealing a room is the correct response to a short, passing outdoor airborne hazard. It is a temporary measure with a hard time limit, and the limit is the part people forget.

steps.text: First decide whether to shelter or to leave. Sealing is for a plume that will pass. If authorities say evacuate, evacuate — a sealed room is not a defence against a sustained release.
Choose an interior room, above ground level for heavier-than-air hazards, with as few windows and doors as possible. Take a radio, water, your phone and medication with you.
Shut off anything that moves outside air in: air conditioning, forced-air heating, bathroom and kitchen extractors. Close the fireplace damper.

Seal the gaps with plastic sheeting and duct tape — around the door, over vents, over windows. Pre-cut the sheeting to size and label each piece now, because doing this under pressure in the dark is how it fails.
Plan on about ten square feet of floor space per person, which gives enough air for several hours in a well-sealed room.
Keep the radio on and stay until authorities say the hazard has passed. They will usually also tell you to then open everything up and ventilate.
steps.caution: A sealed room has a time limit. Carbon dioxide accumulates from breathing, and the better the seal the sooner that matters. This is a measure for hours, not days.

steps.text: Never run any fuel-burning device in a sealed room. The sealing that protects you from the outside is exactly what concentrates combustion products inside.

failureModes.symptom: Headache and drowsiness after some hours
failureModes.cause: Carbon dioxide build-up in a well-sealed small room
failureModes.remedy: This is the time limit arriving. Ventilate if the outside hazard has passed, and follow the radio.

failureModes.symptom: Tape will not hold
failureModes.cause: Dusty or painted surfaces, or sheeting cut too small
failureModes.remedy: Pre-cut and label sheeting in advance, and wipe surfaces before taping.

failureModes.symptom: Sealed in and the hazard did not pass
failureModes.cause: Sealing chosen when evacuation was advised
failureModes.remedy: Follow the instruction given. Sealing is for a passing plume.

doesNotDo: Sealing a room does NOT provide protection for days. Carbon dioxide from breathing sets a hard limit measured in hours.
It does not protect against a sustained release, and it is not an alternative to evacuation when evacuation is advised.
It does not make it safe to run a heater, stove or generator inside — a sealed room concentrates carbon monoxide faster than an unsealed one.
Plastic and tape do not create an airtight seal in a real house. They reduce exchange; they do not eliminate it.
It does nothing for radiation from an external source — distance and shielding mass do that, not plastic sheeting.

title: Dressing for a house with no heating
summary: Clothing is the cheapest heating system you own and the only one that works without fuel. The principles are unglamorous, decades old, and reliably ignored until somebody is cold.

steps.text: Layer in three functions: a thin layer against the skin that moves moisture, an insulating middle layer that traps air, and an outer layer that stops wind. Each does a different job and skipping one is why people are cold in a large coat.
Avoid cotton against the skin in the cold. It absorbs moisture, holds it, and stops insulating. Wool and synthetics keep working damp; cotton does not.
steps.caution: Wet clothing against skin draws heat away many times faster than dry. Getting sweaty inside the house and then sitting still is a real route into cold injury.

steps.text: Vent before you sweat. If you are working — clearing snow, moving water — remove a layer early. Sweat that cools on you afterwards is the problem.
Cover the head, neck and hands. These lose heat disproportionately, and a hat and scarf buy more warmth per gram than another jumper.
Keep feet dry and loose. Tight boots or several tight socks restrict circulation and make cold feet worse rather than better.
Sleep in dry clothes, never the ones you wore all day, and keep tomorrow's clothes in the bed with you so they are warm when you put them on.
Put a layer under you as well as over you when sleeping. Compressed insulation beneath a body does almost nothing; the cold comes up.

failureModes.symptom: Cold despite wearing everything available
failureModes.cause: Cotton base layers, damp clothing, or no wind layer
failureModes.remedy: Dry wool or synthetic next to skin, and something windproof outermost.

failureModes.symptom: Cold feet that will not warm up
failureModes.cause: Too many socks in a boot sized for one pair
failureModes.remedy: Loosen. Circulation does more than insulation at the extremities.

failureModes.symptom: Wakes cold in the night
failureModes.cause: Nothing insulating underneath, or sleeping in day clothes that are slightly damp
failureModes.remedy: Insulate below, change into dry clothes to sleep.

doesNotDo: Clothing does not generate heat. It slows loss. A person who is not eating and not moving will still get cold in excellent clothing.
A single heavy coat does not substitute for layers — it cannot be adjusted, so you sweat in it and then freeze.
Cotton does not insulate when damp, and 'cotton kills' is a mountaineering cliché because it is accurate.
This does not treat someone who is already hypothermic — see the hypothermia page, which is a different procedure.
More socks do not mean warmer feet if they make the boot tight.

title: Running a generator without killing anyone
summary: A portable generator has two ways of killing people who are nowhere near it. One is carbon monoxide, which kills the household. The other is backfeed, which kills the lineworker restoring your power.

steps.text: Outdoors only. Never in a house, a garage, a basement, a crawlspace, a shed or a covered porch — not with the door open, not with a fan running, not for five minutes.

Put the exhaust at least 20 feet from any door, window or vent, pointed away from the building. The Consumer Product Safety Commission is explicit that 20 feet is the figure, and that it applies regardless of a shorter distance in the manufacturer's manual.
steps.caution: Some manuals say five feet. The CPSC's testing says twenty. Use twenty.

steps.text: Fit carbon monoxide alarms indoors on every sleeping level before you ever run the generator.
Run appliances from the generator with heavy-gauge outdoor-rated extension cords, plugged directly into the generator's outlets.

NEVER plug a generator into a wall outlet to power the house. That is backfeed. It energises the utility line outside and can electrocute the lineworker working to restore your supply, and it can destroy your own wiring when the supply returns.
steps.caution: If you want the generator to run house circuits, a licensed electrician installs a transfer switch. There is no safe improvised version of this, and the person it kills is someone else.

steps.text: Let it cool before refuelling. Petrol spilled on a hot engine ignites. Store fuel in approved containers, outside, away from the house and away from any pilot light.
Keep it dry and out of standing water, on a level surface, and keep hands dry when touching it. Run it under an open canopy, never an enclosed one.
Start it once every few months with the fuel you actually have, and run it under load. A generator that has never been started is a heavy object with a pull cord.

failureModes.symptom: Household unwell with headaches while the generator runs
failureModes.cause: Exhaust too close to the building, or wind carrying it to a vent
failureModes.remedy: Everyone outside, call emergency services from outside, and reposition to 20 feet and downwind before any restart.

failureModes.symptom: Generator will not start when needed
failureModes.cause: Stale fuel, varnished carburettor, flat starter battery
failureModes.remedy: Run it quarterly under load, use fuel stabiliser, and keep it serviced.

failureModes.symptom: Breaker trips repeatedly
failureModes.cause: Load exceeds the generator's rating, or a high starting surge from a motor
failureModes.remedy: Add loads one at a time, largest motor first, and total the running watts before plugging anything in.

doesNotDo: A generator in a garage with the door open is NOT safe. This specific arrangement has killed many people and is the most common fatal mistake with these machines.
Backfeeding through a wall outlet does not just risk your own wiring — it can kill a lineworker on the pole. There is no safe improvised version of a transfer switch.
A carbon monoxide alarm does not make a badly placed generator safe. It tells you it is already too late.
A generator does not power a house. It powers a few appliances on cords, unless an electrician has fitted a transfer switch.
A newer generator with a CO shutoff sensor reduces risk but does not remove it, and does not change the 20-foot rule.
