title: Work out what you actually need to power
summary: People buy power capacity before they know what they need it for, and then discover that the big number on the box is not the number that mattered. Do the arithmetic first; it takes twenty minutes and it is almost always reassuring.

steps.text: List only what genuinely must run. For most households that is phones, a light or two, a radio, and any medical device. Everything else is comfort, and comfort can wait a few days.
Find each device's draw in watts, usually on a label or the charger. Multiply watts by the hours you need it, and you have watt-hours — the unit that actually matters.

Add it up per day. A phone is roughly 15 watt-hours for a full charge. An LED lamp might be 5 watts for 5 hours, so 25. A small radio is a couple of watt-hours. Most households land between 50 and 150 watt-hours a day, which is far less than people assume.
Now match that to storage. A 20,000 mAh power bank holds roughly 74 watt-hours, so it covers a day or two of the essential list and several phone charges.

Treat medical equipment separately and first. A CPAP, oxygen concentrator, nebuliser or powered wheelchair has a hard requirement and usually a large one. Talk to the supplier about battery options and register with your utility's medical priority list now.
steps.caution: Do not plan medical power from an estimate. Get the actual draw and the actual runtime from the supplier, and have a plan that does not depend on the grid.

steps.text: Separate the things that need no electricity at all. A hand-crank radio, a mechanical can opener, a paper map and a book remove themselves from the budget entirely.
Decide the order you will shed load in before you need to. Phones and medical first, light second, everything else last.

failureModes.symptom: Power bank flat on day one
failureModes.cause: A laptop or a tablet quietly consuming most of the capacity
failureModes.remedy: Charge phones only, and put the laptop on the non-essential list.

failureModes.symptom: Bought a large battery and still short
failureModes.cause: Sized on peak watts rather than daily watt-hours
failureModes.remedy: Budget in watt-hours per day; it is the number that determines how long you last.

failureModes.symptom: Power bank was flat when the outage started
failureModes.cause: Self-discharge over months
failureModes.remedy: Top it up every three months. Put it in the rotation queue.

doesNotDo: A watt-hour budget does not cover medical equipment adequately — that needs real figures from the device supplier, not an estimate from a label.
It does not account for the surge a motor draws at startup, which can be several times its running draw and is what trips generator breakers.
Capacity printed on a power bank is cell capacity, not delivered capacity. Expect to get roughly two thirds of the headline number out of it.
Cold weather reduces battery capacity substantially, and the figures above assume room temperature.

title: Making a phone last four days
summary: A modern phone will run for days rather than hours if you stop it doing the two things that drain it: holding the screen on, and hunting for a signal that is not there.

steps.text: Charge everything the moment a warning is issued, not when the lights go out. This is the single highest-value minute in the whole topic.
Turn the screen brightness right down and shorten the auto-lock. The display is usually the largest single consumer.
Put it in airplane mode when you are not using it. A phone with no signal burns power searching at full transmit power, and that search is often the second largest drain.
steps.caution: Agree a check-in schedule with your household first — airplane mode means you will not receive calls or emergency alerts while it is on. Come out of it at agreed times.

steps.text: Switch to low-power mode immediately, and turn off background refresh, location services and automatic updates.
Send texts rather than making calls. A text is a tiny burst of data that will often get through a congested network when a voice call will not, and it costs a fraction of the battery.
Use a separate torch. Using the phone as a flashlight is an expensive way to find the bathroom.
Download what you need while you still have a connection: offline maps, your documents, this library. Anything you have to fetch later costs radio time.
Keep the phone warm in cold weather. Battery capacity drops sharply in the cold, and a phone that dies at 40% was simply cold. Inside a coat, not in a pocket against a window.

failureModes.symptom: Battery falls fast despite light use
failureModes.cause: No signal, radio searching at full power
failureModes.remedy: Airplane mode between agreed check-in times.

failureModes.symptom: Phone dies showing 40%
failureModes.cause: Cold
failureModes.remedy: Warm it against your body and it will usually recover some charge.

failureModes.symptom: Power bank will not charge the phone
failureModes.cause: Flat power bank, or a cable that only carries power one way
failureModes.remedy: Top up power banks quarterly and test the actual cable you have stored.

doesNotDo: Saving battery does not create a signal. If the network is down, a full battery does not help you call anyone.
Airplane mode means you will not receive emergency alerts or calls while it is enabled — which is why the check-in schedule matters.
A phone is not a substitute for a weather radio. Cell networks fail in exactly the conditions where you most need the forecast.
This does not help if the phone is your only copy of your plan. Print it.

title: Small solar: what a folding panel will and will not do
summary: A portable panel is genuinely useful for the small loads that matter and routinely oversold for everything else. The rating on the box is a laboratory number you will not see in your garden.

steps.text: Match the panel to the job: keeping phones, lamps, a radio and a power bank going. That is a job a 20 to 100 watt folding panel does well.

Expect substantially less than the rated output. The rating assumes full perpendicular sun, cool panel temperature and a clean surface. Real figures are commonly half to two thirds of that, and much less under cloud or smoke.
Aim it. A panel pointed at the sun produces several times what a flat panel produces, and repointing it two or three times a day is the cheapest performance upgrade available.
Charge a battery, not a device. Direct charging stops every time a cloud passes and some devices handle that badly. Panel to power bank to device is more reliable.
Keep it cool and clean. Panels lose efficiency as they heat, so a small air gap beneath helps, and dust or ash on the surface costs real output.
Do not leave it unattended outdoors in a populated area. It is a visible, portable, valuable object.
Test the full chain — panel, cable, controller, battery, device — before you need it. Mismatched connectors are the most common reason a kit does not work on the day.

failureModes.symptom: Panel produces almost nothing
failureModes.cause: Cloud, smoke, poor angle, or shade across any part of the panel
failureModes.remedy: Reaim it, and clear any partial shading — on many panels a shadow across one cell disproportionately cuts the whole output.

failureModes.symptom: Device charges then stops repeatedly
failureModes.cause: Intermittent cloud and direct device charging
failureModes.remedy: Charge a power bank and run the device from that.

failureModes.symptom: Cables do not fit
failureModes.cause: Connector standards vary between manufacturers
failureModes.remedy: Assemble and test the whole chain before storing it.

doesNotDo: A folding panel does NOT run a house, a fridge, electric heating or well pump. It charges small batteries.
It does not produce its rated wattage in practice. Treat the label as a ceiling you will not reach.
It does not work meaningfully under heavy wildfire smoke, which is exactly the scenario where people reach for it.
It does not charge overnight or through the shortest winter days in any useful quantity.
A panel without a battery is not a power system. The battery is the part that makes it useful.

title: Storing and handling batteries safely
summary: A lithium cell that is damaged, overheated or short-circuited does not simply fail. It vents, burns extremely hot, cannot be smothered, and reignites. The precautions are small and the failure is not.

steps.text: Store loose cells so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. A loose 9V or a lithium cell in a drawer with keys and coins is a fire waiting for contact; tape the terminals or use a case.
Keep batteries cool and dry and out of direct sun. A car glovebox in summer is one of the worst places in your household.
Never mix old and new cells, or different chemistries, in the same device. Mismatched cells drive the weak one into reverse and it leaks or vents.
Remove batteries from anything you are storing for months. Alkaline leakage destroys more torches and radios than any other cause.
Inspect lithium packs for swelling, dents, punctures or a hot charge. A swollen pack is a failed pack: stop using it, do not charge it, and get it out of the house.
steps.caution: Never charge a swollen, punctured or water-damaged lithium battery, and never charge one unattended overnight on a soft surface. Charge on a hard, non-flammable surface where you can see it.

steps.text: Use the charger designed for the cell. Charging lithium cells on an improvised or mismatched charger is a common route to thermal runaway.
For a lithium fire, use large amounts of water to cool it, and call the fire service. Water does not put the reaction out but it carries away heat, which is what stops it spreading.
steps.caution: Do not try to smother a lithium battery fire — it supplies its own oxidiser and will keep burning. Expect it to reignite. Get people out and call emergency services.

steps.text: Dispose of lithium cells at a proper recycling point, never in household waste or kerbside recycling. They start fires in collection trucks and facilities regularly.

failureModes.symptom: Device corroded and dead in storage
failureModes.cause: Alkaline cells left in it
failureModes.remedy: Remove batteries from stored equipment and store them alongside.

failureModes.symptom: Power bank hot or swollen
failureModes.cause: Ageing cells, heat, or a bad charge cycle
failureModes.remedy: Stop using it. Do not charge it. Take it to a recycling point.

failureModes.symptom: Torch flat despite rarely being used
failureModes.cause: Self-discharge, or a switch nudged on in a bag
failureModes.remedy: Lithium primary cells for long storage, and store the torch with a battery reversed so it cannot switch on.

doesNotDo: Smothering a lithium fire does NOT put it out. The cell supplies its own oxidiser; water is for cooling and the fire service is for the rest.
A battery that looks fine is not necessarily fine. Internal damage from a drop may not show on the outside.
Freezing a battery does not restore capacity and may damage it. Cold reduces available capacity temporarily, not permanently.
Alkaline and lithium cells are not interchangeable in every device — voltage curves differ, and some electronics object.
This does not cover vehicle or home storage batteries, which are a different scale of hazard entirely.

title: Handwashing when water is scarce
summary: In a prolonged outage, the thing most likely to make your household ill is not the water supply or the food. It is hands. Handwashing is the single highest-return action in this entire library and it is the first thing that gets skipped.

steps.text: Soap and water first, every time it is available. Soap physically lifts organisms off skin and the rinse carries them away — that mechanism works on things alcohol does not touch.

Wash at the moments that matter: before preparing or eating food, after using the toilet or handling waste, after handling anything from floodwater, after caring for someone ill, and after handling animals.

Use very little water with a tippy-tap: a bottle or jug with a small hole, hung so it trickles. Wet hands, turn it off, lather twenty seconds, rinse briefly. A litre washes many pairs of hands this way.
Catch the greywater in a basin and use it to flush, rather than letting it soak away.
Use alcohol sanitiser of at least 60% when soap and water genuinely are not available. Cover all surfaces of both hands and rub until dry — about twenty seconds.
Wash rather than sanitise when hands are visibly dirty or greasy. Alcohol works poorly through soil and grease.
steps.caution: Alcohol sanitiser is not effective against some of the organisms most likely to circulate in a sanitation emergency, including norovirus and Cryptosporidium. When those are a risk, soap and water are the answer.

steps.text: Put the handwashing station where the activity is — next to the bucket toilet and next to the food preparation area, at arm's reach. Distance is the entire reason people skip it.

failureModes.symptom: Household illness spreading despite clean water and food
failureModes.cause: Hand-to-mouth transmission, almost always
failureModes.remedy: Station at the point of use, and treat it as the household's one non-negotiable rule.

failureModes.symptom: Soap runs out
failureModes.cause: Bar soap used for everything
failureModes.remedy: Store more than feels reasonable. It is light, cheap and lasts indefinitely.

failureModes.symptom: People use sanitiser instead of washing
failureModes.cause: It is easier and the station is inconvenient
failureModes.remedy: Make washing the easy option by moving the station, not by exhortation.

doesNotDo: Hand sanitiser does NOT replace soap and water. It is less effective on visibly soiled hands and does not work well against norovirus or Cryptosporidium — two of the most likely organisms in a sanitation emergency.
Washing does not sterilise your hands. It reduces the load, which is enough.
Sanitiser below 60% alcohol is substantially less effective, and some products marketed as sanitiser contain none.
Gloves are not a substitute for washing. They become contaminated exactly as hands do, and people touch their face through them.
Washing does not help if the water you rinse with is contaminated — use treated water for the final rinse where the supply is in doubt.

title: Disinfecting surfaces with bleach, and why it is not the water ratio
summary: Bleach appears twice in emergency guidance at two wildly different strengths, and the two get confused constantly. The dose that disinfects a worktop is dozens of times stronger than the dose that makes water drinkable.

steps.text: Know which job you are doing. Treating drinking water is roughly 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon. Disinfecting a surface is roughly a third of a cup per gallon — a vastly stronger solution.
steps.caution: Never drink surface-disinfection solution, and never expect water-treatment dosing to disinfect a surface. Mixing these up in either direction causes harm: one poisons, the other leaves you thinking a surface is clean when it is not.

steps.text: Clean before you disinfect. Visible soil, grease and organic matter consume chlorine and shield organisms beneath. Wash with soap and water first, always.
Mix fresh. A bleach solution loses strength within about a day, faster in light and warmth. Yesterday's bottle is mostly salt water.
Let it sit. Contact time is doing the work — leave the surface visibly wet for at least a minute, longer for a rougher surface, then air dry or rinse food surfaces with safe water.
Ventilate, and wear gloves and eye protection. Bleach damages skin, eyes and airways at disinfection strength.
NEVER mix bleach with ammonia, with any acid including vinegar, or with any other cleaning product.
steps.caution: Bleach and ammonia produce chloramine gas. Bleach and acid produce chlorine gas. Both have killed people cleaning in poorly ventilated rooms, and this happens most often during the cleanup after a flood.

steps.text: After floodwater, discard rather than disinfect anything porous that was soaked: upholstered furniture, mattresses, carpet, particleboard, and most soft toys. They cannot be reliably disinfected.

failureModes.symptom: Surfaces disinfected but illness continues
failureModes.cause: Soil not cleaned off first, or contact time too short
failureModes.remedy: Clean, then disinfect, then leave it wet for a full minute.

failureModes.symptom: Solution seems to do nothing
failureModes.cause: Old bleach, or solution mixed days ago
failureModes.remedy: Replace stored bleach annually and mix fresh each day.

failureModes.symptom: Coughing and burning eyes while cleaning
failureModes.cause: Product mixing, or poor ventilation
failureModes.remedy: Leave the area, get fresh air, and never combine cleaning products.

doesNotDo: Surface disinfection strength is NOT safe to drink, and water-treatment strength does NOT disinfect surfaces. These are different operations with different doses and confusing them is the central hazard of this topic.
Bleach does not work through dirt. Cleaning first is not optional, it is what makes the disinfection effective.
A bleach solution does not keep. It is substantially weaker within a day.
Disinfecting does not rescue porous items soaked in floodwater — they are discarded, not cleaned.
Scented, splash-less, gel and cleaner-added bleaches are not suitable for disinfection dosing in the way plain sodium hypochlorite is, and they are never suitable for water.

title: Greywater: using the same litre three times
summary: Washing water is not drinking water and it is not sewage. Used in the right order it does three jobs, and ignoring it is how a household with plenty of stored water still runs out.

steps.text: Work down the cleanliness ladder, never up. Rinse water from dishes or hands becomes wash water for floors; floor water becomes flush water. The same litre does three jobs on the way down.
Catch it. A basin in the sink and a bucket in the shower collect water that otherwise goes down the drain while your stored supply is shrinking.
Keep food-preparation rinse water separate from anything that has touched bodies or cleaning. Clean to dirty, one direction only.
Use it within a day. Greywater with food particles and warmth grows bacteria quickly and will smell within hours in summer.
Use plain, low-phosphate, unscented soap if you intend to put greywater on soil, and keep it off anything you will eat.
steps.caution: Do not put greywater on vegetables you will eat raw, do not let it pool where children or pets play, and never discharge it into a watercourse or near a well head.

steps.text: Do not store greywater for more than a day, and never store it in a container that could be mistaken for drinking water. Label it clearly.
If the sewer itself is compromised, stop putting anything down the drain at all and switch fully to the bucket system — including greywater, which will back up through the same failed line.

failureModes.symptom: House smells within a day
failureModes.cause: Greywater stored too long, or food particles in it
failureModes.remedy: Use it the same day, strain food solids out, and keep containers covered.

failureModes.symptom: Someone drinks from the greywater container
failureModes.cause: Unlabelled clear water in a familiar container
failureModes.remedy: Label every container, and never use a drinking-water container for greywater.

failureModes.symptom: Drains back up
failureModes.cause: Sewer compromised while greywater is still going down it
failureModes.remedy: Stop all drain use and switch entirely to buckets.

doesNotDo: Greywater is not drinking water, and no amount of settling or straining makes it so. It carries soap, grease, food and skin bacteria.
It is not safe for watering food crops you eat raw.
It does not keep. A day is the practical limit before it becomes a smell and a health problem of its own.
Reusing it does not help if the sewer line itself has failed — then it has nowhere to go.
It does not replace the bucket toilet. Greywater and blackwater are different problems and must stay separate.

title: Waste over weeks, not days
summary: The twin-bucket system buys you weeks. The limiting factor is not the buckets, it is where the sealed bags go, and households discover that at about day ten.

steps.text: Work out the volume before you need to. An adult produces roughly a litre of solid waste a week, plus cover material, plus bag. For a household of four over a month that is a meaningful pile, and it has to go somewhere.
Designate the storage location now: outside, shaded, off the ground, in a secondary sealed container such as a lidded bin, away from where people walk, children play and food is prepared.
Double-bag, seal each bag individually, and do not overfill — a bag that splits during handling is the worst moment in this entire topic.
Keep cover material coming. Budget roughly a gallon per person per week, and have a resupply plan: sawdust from a timber yard, leaf mould, dry soil, shredded paper.
Follow local authority instructions for disposal as soon as they are issued. Most jurisdictions set up collection points after an event, and that is the correct destination.

If burial is genuinely the only option and authorities permit it, site it at least 200 feet from any well, spring, watercourse or garden bed, downhill of any water source, and at least two feet deep with soil over it.
steps.caution: Never burn human waste, and never compost it in an ordinary garden heap. Neither reaches a temperature that reliably kills pathogens, and burning disperses them.

steps.text: Keep urine separate throughout and dispose of it separately — it is the bulk of the volume and much less hazardous, and separating it roughly halves the storage problem.
Handle bags with gloves, wash hands immediately afterwards, and keep a dedicated set of outer clothing or gloves for the job.

failureModes.symptom: Running out of storage space around day ten
failureModes.cause: Only the bucket was planned, not the destination
failureModes.remedy: Designate and prepare the secondary storage before the event, and separate urine to halve the volume.

failureModes.symptom: Flies and smell at the storage point
failureModes.cause: Bags not sealed individually, or storage in sun
failureModes.remedy: Seal each bag, store in a lidded bin, keep it shaded.

failureModes.symptom: Cover material gone by the end of week one
failureModes.cause: Universally underestimated
failureModes.remedy: A gallon per person per week, plus a resupply source identified in advance.

doesNotDo: This does not treat or sterilise waste. It contains it. The bags stay hazardous until properly disposed of.
Burning does not make it safe and disperses pathogens in smoke. Ordinary garden composting does not reach a temperature that kills them.
It does not work indefinitely — it buys weeks, bounded entirely by storage space.
It does not address a failed sewer line, which also affects every drain in the house including greywater.
Burial is not permitted everywhere and is not a default. Follow local authority instruction first.

title: Staying clean enough, including the parts nobody plans for
summary: Menstruation does not pause for an emergency, incontinence does not either, and neither appears on most preparedness lists. Planning for them costs almost nothing and their absence causes real distress and real infection risk.

steps.text: Stock menstrual supplies for at least the household's target horizon, plus margin. Stress can bring periods forward, make them heavier, or trigger one unexpectedly.
Include both disposable and reusable options. Reusables need water to clean; disposables need somewhere to put them. Having both means neither constraint traps you.
Plan disposal: sealed bags into the solid waste stream, never down a toilet that may not be flushing, and never into greywater.
Stock incontinence supplies for anyone who needs them, at the same depth as medication. Running out is both a dignity problem and a skin-infection problem.
Sponge-bathe rather than shower. A basin, a litre of warm water, a cloth and soap cleans a person properly. Prioritise hands, face, armpits, groin and feet, in that order.
Keep feet dry and change socks. Trench foot and fungal infection are genuine cold and wet-weather casualties and they disable people quietly.
steps.caution: Skin that stays wet breaks down. For anyone immobile or incontinent, keeping skin clean and dry is the difference between discomfort and a pressure sore that needs medical care.

steps.text: Keep a small privacy provision in the plan — a sheet, a tarp, a corner. Dignity is not a luxury over a two-week event and its absence stops people drinking and using the toilet when they should.
Pack for this in the go bag too, not only the home kit. Evacuation does not pause it either.

failureModes.symptom: Supplies run out mid-event
failureModes.cause: Planned for an average cycle rather than a stressed one
failureModes.remedy: Overstock. It is light, cheap and stores indefinitely.

failureModes.symptom: Skin breakdown in someone immobile
failureModes.cause: Wet skin, infrequent changing, no washing water allocated
failureModes.remedy: Allocate water for hygiene specifically, change and dry regularly, and seek medical help early.

failureModes.symptom: People stop drinking enough
failureModes.cause: Avoiding an unpleasant or non-private toilet
failureModes.remedy: Make the toilet tolerable and private. It is a hydration intervention as much as a dignity one.

doesNotDo: This does not cover medical treatment of infection. Skin breakdown, a urinary infection or a wound that is not healing needs a clinician, not a hygiene routine.
Sponge-bathing does not substitute for proper washing over long periods, particularly for anyone immobile.
Hand sanitiser is not body-cleaning and should not be used as such — it dries and damages skin.
Reusable products do not help when water is the binding constraint, which is why both kinds belong in the store.

title: A first aid kit that matches the likely injuries
summary: Most bought kits are a hundred plasters and nothing that handles the injuries an outage actually produces: deep cuts from broken glass, burns, sprains and the slow problems of people who cannot reach a pharmacy.

steps.text: Start from the likely injuries, not from a kit list. In a storm or outage those are lacerations from glass and debris, burns from improvised cooking and heating, falls and sprains in the dark, and chronic conditions going unmanaged.
Stock enough bleeding control to matter: several sterile gauze pads, roller bandages, and at least one proper trauma dressing. A box of small plasters does not address a bleeding wound.
Include irrigation. A large syringe or a squeeze bottle for flushing a wound with clean water does more to prevent infection than any ointment.
Add the unglamorous items people actually run out of: disposable gloves, tape, scissors or shears, tweezers, a thermometer, elastic wrap for sprains, burn dressings, and eye wash.

Write a household medication list and keep a copy in the kit: everyone's prescriptions by generic name, doses as prescribed, allergies, conditions, and the prescriber's details. This single page is the most useful thing in the kit if you reach a clinician who has never met you.

Keep a surplus of each maintenance medication, arranged in advance with the prescriber, and rotate it so it never expires. This is the highest-value medical item in the household for anyone who takes something daily.
Take a class. Bleeding control and CPR are taught in a couple of hours, widely and cheaply, and reading about them is not the same thing.
steps.caution: A kit is equipment, not capability. Items you have never used will not help you under stress.

steps.text: Check it twice a year against the rotation queue: expired items out, used items replaced, batteries in the torch.

failureModes.symptom: Kit opened and nothing in it fits the problem
failureModes.cause: A retail kit built for paper cuts
failureModes.remedy: Build around real injuries: bleeding, burns, sprains, chronic conditions.

failureModes.symptom: Nobody knows how to use the contents
failureModes.cause: Equipment bought, training skipped
failureModes.remedy: A bleeding-control and CPR class for at least two people in the household.

failureModes.symptom: Everything in it expired
failureModes.cause: Kit treated as a purchase rather than a stock
failureModes.remedy: Put the kit in the rotation queue with a date.

doesNotDo: A kit does not make anyone capable. Equipment without training is weight.
It does not substitute for emergency medical care, and nothing in it treats a serious injury — it buys time.

It does not cover prescription medicine. This library covers what a trained layperson can do. It does not cover invasive procedures, and it gives no dosing guidance for any prescription or controlled medicine.
It does not replace a written medication list, which is often more use to a clinician than anything else you carry.
A kit in the car is not a kit in the house. Injuries happen where you are.

title: Stopping serious bleeding
summary: Someone bleeding heavily from a limb can die in minutes, which is less time than an ambulance usually takes even on a good day. This is the one medical skill where an untrained bystander most reliably saves a life, and it is taught in two hours.

steps.text: Make sure the scene is safe for you first. A second casualty helps nobody.
Call 911 or send someone to call. Do this before you start, or while you work if you are alone with a phone on speaker.
Find the bleeding. Clothing hides a great deal — expose the wound rather than guessing from the outside.
Press hard, directly on the wound, with both hands, using a cloth or dressing if available and your hands if not. Most bleeding stops with firm, sustained, direct pressure.
steps.caution: Hard means hard, and sustained means you do not lift it to look. Checking whether it has worked restarts the bleeding.

steps.text: If it is a deep wound you can pack, press gauze or clean cloth firmly into the wound cavity and keep pressing from outside.

If the bleeding is from a limb and direct pressure is not controlling it, apply a tourniquet high and tight — a few inches above the wound, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, which will hurt.
steps.caution: Write down the time you applied it. Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet once applied; that is a decision for the people who take over. A correctly applied tourniquet is painful, and pain is not a reason to release it.

steps.text: Keep the person warm and lying down, keep talking to them, and keep the pressure on until someone takes over.
Learn this properly. Bleeding control is taught free or cheaply through widely available classes and it is a different thing in your hands than on a page.

failureModes.symptom: Bleeding restarts every time it seems to stop
failureModes.cause: Pressure lifted to check
failureModes.remedy: Do not lift. Add dressing on top of soaked dressing and keep pressing.

failureModes.symptom: Tourniquet does not stop the bleeding
failureModes.cause: Not tight enough, or placed over a joint
failureModes.remedy: Tighten further, or place a second one above the first. It must be tight enough to stop arterial flow.

failureModes.symptom: Rescuer becomes a casualty
failureModes.cause: Scene not assessed — glass, live wire, unstable structure
failureModes.remedy: Check the scene first, every time.

doesNotDo: This does not treat internal bleeding, which you cannot see and cannot press on. Suspect it after any significant impact and get emergency help.
A tourniquet is for limbs only. It does nothing for bleeding from the torso, neck, armpit or groin — there, press and pack.
Stopping bleeding does not treat shock, which can still kill afterwards. Keep them warm and flat and get help.

This page is not a substitute for a hands-on class, and This library covers what a trained layperson can do. It does not cover invasive procedures, and it gives no dosing guidance for any prescription or controlled medicine.
It does not cover what to do when help is not coming at all, which is a different and much harder situation.

title: Cleaning a wound when the pharmacy is shut
summary: After a storm or a flood the cuts are dirtier than usual, the water is worse than usual, and medical care is further away than usual. Infection, not the original injury, is what turns a minor wound into a serious problem.

steps.text: Wash your own hands first, and wear gloves if you have them.
Control any bleeding before you think about cleaning.

Irrigate the wound with a large volume of clean drinking water — more than feels necessary, under some pressure from a syringe or squeezed bottle. Volume and pressure are what remove contamination; dabbing does not.
steps.caution: Use water you would drink. Irrigating a wound with untreated floodwater or river water introduces exactly the organisms you are trying to remove.

steps.text: Wash the surrounding skin with soap and water. Soap around the wound, clean water in it.
Do not pour hydrogen peroxide, alcohol or iodine into an open wound. They damage the tissue that has to heal and do not improve outcomes compared with thorough irrigation.
steps.caution: This is widespread household practice and it is wrong. Clean water, in quantity, is the better tool.

steps.text: Remove visible debris you can reach easily with clean tweezers. Leave anything embedded deeply, and leave any object that has penetrated and stayed in — removing it can restart serious bleeding.
Cover with a clean dry dressing and change it daily, or sooner if it becomes wet or dirty.
Watch for infection: spreading redness, increasing pain after the first day, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks running from the wound, or fever. Any of those means find a clinician.
steps.caution: Seek care promptly for any wound from floodwater, any animal or human bite, any puncture wound, any wound you cannot get clean, and if your tetanus vaccination is not up to date. Wounds contaminated with floodwater carry organisms that household care will not handle.

failureModes.symptom: Wound looks worse on day two or three
failureModes.cause: Infection establishing, or incomplete initial cleaning
failureModes.remedy: Seek medical care. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

failureModes.symptom: Wound keeps reopening
failureModes.cause: Over a joint, or dressing not supporting it
failureModes.remedy: Immobilise the area and keep it covered, and get it assessed if it will not close.

failureModes.symptom: Healing slowly with no obvious infection
failureModes.cause: Diabetes, poor circulation, or the wound being kept too dry or too wet
failureModes.remedy: Anyone with diabetes or circulatory problems should treat any wound as needing professional review early.

doesNotDo: Hydrogen peroxide, alcohol and iodine do NOT belong in an open wound. They damage healing tissue and do not outperform thorough irrigation with clean water.
Cleaning does not substitute for stitches, antibiotics or a tetanus booster where those are needed.
This does not cover deep, gaping, heavily contaminated or penetrating wounds, animal bites, or anything involving a joint, nerve, tendon or bone. Those need a clinician.
It does not cover burns, which have different handling, or chemical exposure to the skin.
This library covers what a trained layperson can do. It does not cover invasive procedures, and it gives no dosing guidance for any prescription or controlled medicine.

title: Not running out of the medicine you take every day
summary: In most real emergencies, the serious medical problems are not injuries. They are the ordinary chronic conditions of people who could not reach a pharmacy — and that is the most preventable harm in this entire library.

steps.text: Ask your prescriber for a surplus, explicitly for emergency preparedness. Many will arrange it, and some insurers permit an early refill for this purpose. Ask well before you need it.

Write the list down and keep a copy in the document pouch and another with your out-of-area contact: every medicine by generic name, the dose as prescribed, what it is for, allergies, conditions, and your prescriber and pharmacy details.
Know the generic names. In a disrupted supply chain, or at a shelter, or out of state, the brand you use may not be what is available and the generic name is what a pharmacist can act on.
Keep medicines in the original labelled containers. The label is what lets another clinician or pharmacist confirm what you take.

Plan for anything refrigerated. Insulin and some other medicines have specific temperature requirements and a defined tolerance outside them — get those figures from your pharmacist and plan cool storage for a power cut.
steps.caution: Do not guess at how long a refrigerated medicine remains usable, and do not assume it is ruined either. Ask your pharmacist for the actual figure for your specific product, and write it on the list.

steps.text: Know your pharmacy's emergency procedure. Many states allow emergency refills during a declared disaster, and most chains can access your record from another branch.
Register with your utility's medical priority list if anyone depends on powered equipment, and tell your local emergency services if that is offered where you live.
Rotate the surplus so it never expires, and keep a few days of it in the go bag as well as the home store.

failureModes.symptom: Surplus expired unused
failureModes.cause: Set aside and forgotten
failureModes.remedy: Rotate it into normal use and replace. Put it in the rotation queue.

failureModes.symptom: Evacuated without medication
failureModes.cause: It lives in a bathroom cabinet, not the grab bag
failureModes.remedy: A few days' supply in the go bag, and the written list in the document pouch.

failureModes.symptom: Pharmacy cannot help out of state
failureModes.cause: No record of what you take
failureModes.remedy: The written list with generic names solves this almost entirely.

doesNotDo: This page gives NO dosing guidance, no advice on changing, splitting, stopping or stretching any medicine, and no advice on substitutes. This library covers what a trained layperson can do. It does not cover invasive procedures, and it gives no dosing guidance for any prescription or controlled medicine.
It does not tell you how long a refrigerated medicine stays usable — that is specific to the product and comes from your pharmacist.
It does not cover controlled substances, which have additional legal restrictions on early refills and quantities that vary by state.
Having a surplus does not replace medical care. A condition that is deteriorating needs a clinician, not a larger stock.
It does not cover what to do if you do run out, which is a question for a pharmacist or clinician and not for a checklist.

title: When the ambulance is hours away
summary: In a wide-area event the emergency system is saturated and response times stretch from minutes to hours or longer. Knowing that in advance changes what you do in the first ten minutes, which is the part you control.

steps.text: Call anyway. Even when the system is overwhelmed, calling puts you in the queue, gets you dispatcher instruction, and is how they know you exist. Text to 911 where it is available can get through when voice cannot.

Do the things that work in the first minutes and matter most: stop serious bleeding, open an airway, start CPR if there are no signs of life, get them warm and flat. These are the interventions a layperson can actually deliver.

Write down what happened and when. Time of injury, what you did, times of any tourniquet, what the person took and when, how their condition has changed. Handing that over saves the clinician enormous time.

Decide early whether to wait or to transport. If the route is passable and the hospital is receiving, self-transport is often faster in a saturated system — but ask the dispatcher, because hospitals may be diverting or closed.
Do not move anyone with a suspected spinal injury unless they are in immediate danger where they lie.
steps.caution: Moving someone with a possible spinal injury can cause permanent harm. Immediate danger means fire, flood or collapse — not discomfort.

steps.text: Keep the radio on. Authorities broadcast which facilities are open, which routes are passable, and where aid stations have been set up.

Accept the boundary. There is a point past which a household cannot help and the honest answer is to keep them comfortable, keep calling, and keep trying to reach care. Knowing where that line is prevents people doing harm trying to cross it.
Plan it before the day: which hospitals, which routes, who drives, who stays with the children, and where the medication list is.

failureModes.symptom: Nobody called because the line was assumed to be busy
failureModes.cause: Reasonable assumption, wrong decision
failureModes.remedy: Always call or text. Being in the queue is worth a great deal.

failureModes.symptom: Arrived at a closed or diverting hospital
failureModes.cause: Facilities change status during a large event
failureModes.remedy: Confirm by radio or dispatcher before setting out.

failureModes.symptom: Clinician has to start from nothing on arrival
failureModes.cause: No record of events, times or medications
failureModes.remedy: Write it down as you go, and keep the household medication list current.

doesNotDo: This does not teach you to practise medicine. This library covers what a trained layperson can do. It does not cover invasive procedures, and it gives no dosing guidance for any prescription or controlled medicine.
It does not cover any invasive procedure, suturing, medication administration, or anything beyond what a trained layperson can do.
It does not replace a hands-on first aid and CPR class, which is the single best preparation for this situation.
It does not promise a good outcome. Some injuries and illnesses are not survivable without a hospital, and pretending otherwise would be a cruelty.
It does not cover mental health crisis, which has its own urgent pathways and should be treated as a medical emergency.

title: The radio that works when nothing else does
summary: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts continuously from transmitters that are not your cell network and do not depend on it. It is the most reliable warning channel available to a household and almost nobody owns one.

steps.text: Get a receiver with battery backup and ideally a hand crank, and test it where you actually live — reception varies and a radio that works at the shop may not work in your basement.
Find your local transmitter frequency from the NWS site and set it now. Doing this during a warning is doing it too late.

Set the SAME codes for your county and the neighbouring ones you care about. Specific Area Message Encoding means the radio stays silent until something concerns your area, which is what makes it bearable to leave on.
Enable the alert tone and leave the radio on standby overnight during any watch. A warning at 3am is the entire reason this device exists.
Learn the difference between a watch and a warning. A watch means conditions are favourable — get ready. A warning means it is happening or imminent — act now.
Keep spare batteries with it, and test the alert function monthly. NWS runs a weekly required test, usually Wednesday, which is a free check that your setup works.
Treat it as one of several channels. Wireless Emergency Alerts on a phone, local broadcast radio and an outdoor siren all have different failure modes, and having more than one is the point.

failureModes.symptom: Radio never alerts
failureModes.cause: SAME codes not programmed, alert disabled, or out of transmitter range
failureModes.remedy: Programme the codes, enable the tone, and confirm against the weekly test.

failureModes.symptom: Alerts constantly for irrelevant areas
failureModes.cause: No SAME filtering
failureModes.remedy: Set your county codes; an unfiltered radio gets switched off, which defeats it.

failureModes.symptom: Dead when needed
failureModes.cause: Batteries left in for years
failureModes.remedy: Rotate batteries and keep a crank model as backup.

doesNotDo: A weather radio does not transmit. It cannot call for help and it is not two-way.
It does not cover every hazard everywhere — coverage has gaps, particularly in mountainous terrain.
It does not replace local official channels for non-weather emergencies, though it does carry all-hazards messages.
A phone app is not an equivalent. Cell networks fail in exactly the conditions where the warning matters most.

title: Getting a message out on a failing network
summary: Networks rarely fail completely. They congest, which looks like failure if you only try to make voice calls — and a text will often get through the same tower at the same moment that a call will not.

steps.text: Text, do not call. A text is a tiny packet that retries automatically until it finds a gap. A voice call needs a continuous channel held open and is the first thing congestion denies.

Call your out-of-area contact rather than each other. Local circuits saturate first; a long-distance call often routes around the congested area, and one relay point beats six people calling six people.
Keep calls short if you do get through. Every extra minute occupies a channel somebody else needs.
Use wifi calling where any internet connection survives. A working router on a generator or battery can carry calls when the cell network cannot.
Know that 911 still works in ways you may not expect: a phone with no service and no SIM can still usually dial 911, and text-to-911 is available in many areas.
steps.caution: Text-to-911 is not available everywhere. Where it is not, you get a bounce-back message. Call if you can; text only if you cannot.

steps.text: Send your status once, clearly, to the relay: where you are, whether you are hurt, what you need, and when you will next check in. Then stop transmitting and conserve battery.
Agree the check-in schedule in advance. Fixed times mean phones can be off in between, which is the single biggest battery saving available.
Have a non-electronic fallback: the rally points on the printed card, and a note on the door of where you have gone.

failureModes.symptom: Calls fail repeatedly
failureModes.cause: Congestion, not outage
failureModes.remedy: Switch to text and to the out-of-area relay.

failureModes.symptom: Battery gone by evening
failureModes.cause: Repeated call attempts and the radio searching at full power
failureModes.remedy: Airplane mode between agreed check-ins.

failureModes.symptom: Nobody knows where anyone is
failureModes.cause: No agreed relay and no agreed times
failureModes.remedy: One out-of-area contact, fixed check-in times, and the printed card.

doesNotDo: None of this creates a signal. If the towers are down or have no power, texting does not help.
Text-to-911 is not available in every jurisdiction, and a text to 911 carries less location information than a call.
Social media check-in features do not notify emergency services and are not a substitute for calling.
A phone is not a plan. The printed rally card works when every part of this does not.

title: Two-way radio for a household
summary: Handheld radios are genuinely useful over short distances and genuinely oversold on the packaging. The thirty-mile claim on the box assumes two people on neighbouring mountaintops with nothing in between.

steps.text: Set expectations by terrain, not by the box. In a town or wooded terrain, a handheld FRS radio gives you roughly half a mile to two miles. Line of sight is what matters; radio does not bend around hills or buildings.

Know the licensing. FRS requires no licence and uses fixed low-power handhelds. GMRS allows more power and better antennas but requires an FCC licence, which needs no exam and covers your immediate family. Amateur radio requires passing an exam.
steps.caution: Operating on GMRS or amateur frequencies without the required licence is a violation of FCC rules. Get the licence in advance — the GMRS one is straightforward and lasts years.

steps.text: Agree channels and a schedule in advance: a primary channel, a backup, and fixed times to listen. Radios left on all day flatten batteries for nothing.
Teach everyone the basics: press, pause, then speak, because the first fraction of a second is lost. Say who you are calling and who you are. Keep it short.
Assume anyone can hear you. These are open channels with no privacy, and the 'privacy codes' on consumer radios do not encrypt anything — they only filter what your own radio plays.
steps.caution: Never pass addresses, plans or anything about what you have stored over an open channel.

steps.text: Gain height for range. A few metres of elevation does more than any amount of extra power on a handheld.
Practise before you need it, with the people who will use it, in the places you would actually use it.

failureModes.symptom: Range far below the box claim
failureModes.cause: Buildings, trees and terrain. The claim is a mountaintop figure
failureModes.remedy: Plan around half a mile to two miles, and find height.

failureModes.symptom: Cannot hear each other despite being close
failureModes.cause: Different channels, or mismatched privacy codes
failureModes.remedy: Write the channel and code on a card taped to each radio.

failureModes.symptom: Batteries flat
failureModes.cause: Radios left in transmit-ready standby all day
failureModes.remedy: Scheduled listening windows, and spare batteries.

doesNotDo: A handheld radio does NOT reach thirty miles in any realistic terrain. The packaging figure assumes an unobstructed line of sight.
Privacy codes do not make a transmission private. Anyone scanning the channel hears everything you say.
FRS radios do not reach emergency services. They are household-to-household, not a way to call for help.
A radio does not work without a licensed operator on the frequencies that require one, and the rules are enforced.
This does not cover antenna building, repeater operation or anything requiring an amateur licence — that is a hobby with its own training path.

title: Navigating on paper
summary: A paper map does not need a battery, a signal or a satellite, and it shows you the whole area at once rather than a moving arrow in a two-inch window. The skill it needs is small and perishable.

steps.text: Buy the maps now: a street atlas for your county and the counties you would evacuate through, and a topographic sheet if you are rural. Keep them in the car and in the go bag.
Mark them by hand before anything happens: home, work, schools, all three rally points, your out-of-area destination, hospitals, and the two evacuation routes with their alternates.
Orient the map to the ground. Turn the map until its features line up with what you can see — not north-up, but matching-reality-up. Almost every navigation error starts here.
Learn to read the scale and estimate distance, and learn roughly how long a mile takes you on foot with a loaded bag. Most people badly overestimate how far they can walk in a day carrying weight.
If you have a compass, learn to set the declination for your area and take a simple bearing. If you do not, terrain and roads will carry you most of the way.
Plan routes by handrails — a river, a ridge, a rail line, a major road. A feature you cannot miss is worth more than a precise bearing when you are tired.
Protect the map. A laminated map or a zip bag survives rain; a paper one in a pocket does not last a day.
Walk one of your routes. Every planned route contains at least one surprise — a fence, a culvert, a private road — and the time to find it is now.

failureModes.symptom: Confidently walked the wrong way
failureModes.cause: Map not oriented to the ground
failureModes.remedy: Orient first, every single time you stop.

failureModes.symptom: Route impassable
failureModes.cause: Map out of date, or a feature that only exists on the ground
failureModes.remedy: Always have an alternate, and walk the route once in advance.

failureModes.symptom: Map destroyed by rain
failureModes.cause: Paper, in a pocket
failureModes.remedy: Laminate it or bag it.

doesNotDo: A map does not tell you where you are. It tells you what is there; locating yourself on it is the skill.
It does not show current conditions — a road on the map may be flooded, closed, blocked or gone.
A road atlas does not show terrain, which matters a great deal on foot. A topographic sheet does.
It does not update. A map several years old will be wrong about new development and sometimes about roads.
This does not cover wilderness navigation, which is a deeper skill with its own training.

title: Sleeping badly, on purpose, well
summary: Sleep is the first thing an emergency takes and the thing whose loss does most damage to everything else. Judgement, patience, coordination and immune function all degrade on short sleep, and the person affected is the last to notice.

steps.text: Treat sleep as a logistical requirement, not a luxury. Schedule it the way you schedule water. In any event lasting more than a day, someone who has not slept is a liability rather than an asset.
Rotate watches if someone must stay awake. Short shifts, handed over properly, beat one person staying up all night and being useless the next day.
Keep a wind-down even when everything is wrong. Same order of small actions, lights down, no bright screens. The ritual is what signals sleep when the environment does not.
Deal with cold before you lie down. Shivering prevents sleep, and insulation underneath matters more than blankets on top.
Take naps without guilt. Twenty minutes recovers a meaningful amount of alertness and costs almost nothing.
Accept broken sleep. Several short periods are worse than one long one and far better than none. Lying down and resting with eyes closed has real value even without sleeping.
Be cautious with caffeine late and with alcohol at any point. Alcohol brings sleep on and then fragments it badly, and in the cold it is actively dangerous.
Make the big decisions in the morning. If a decision can wait until after sleep, let it.

failureModes.symptom: Short tempers and poor decisions on day three
failureModes.cause: Accumulated sleep debt
failureModes.remedy: Enforce sleep as a rota. Name it as the cause when it happens; it defuses a great deal.

failureModes.symptom: Cannot sleep despite exhaustion
failureModes.cause: Cold, adrenaline, or no routine
failureModes.remedy: Warm first, insulate underneath, keep the wind-down ritual.

failureModes.symptom: One person doing every night watch
failureModes.cause: Well-meant, unsustainable
failureModes.remedy: Rotate. The watch-keeper is also a resource to be managed.

doesNotDo: This does not treat insomnia, trauma-related sleep disruption or any sleep disorder, all of which need proper care.
It does not address medication for sleep, which is outside this library's scope entirely.
Good sleep hygiene does not compensate for genuine sleep deprivation — only sleep does.
Resting with your eyes closed is not equivalent to sleeping. It helps; it is not a replacement.

title: Keeping a household working together
summary: Most groups that come apart in a prolonged emergency do not come apart over the emergency. They come apart over chores, fairness and someone's tone, and all three are symptoms of exhaustion rather than causes.

steps.text: Name roles early and out loud. Who decides, who cooks, who manages water, who looks after the children, who takes the night watch. Ambiguity is where resentment grows.

Rotate the unpleasant jobs on a visible schedule. The bucket toilet, the night watch and the washing up cause more trouble than any strategic question, and a written rota removes the argument entirely.
Decide openly and explain the reason. People accept hard decisions they understand far more readily than easy ones announced without explanation.
Give everyone a job, including children. Useful work is the most effective anxiety treatment available in these conditions and costs nothing.
Check for the real cause before responding to the argument. Hunger, cold, thirst, needing the toilet and sleep debt account for the large majority of conflict. Feed everyone and reconvene.
Make space for people to be alone. Enforced proximity with no privacy is genuinely hard, and twenty minutes apart prevents a great deal.
Hold a short daily check-in at a fixed time: what happened, what we are doing today, what each person needs. Predictability is calming in itself.
Apologise quickly and move on. Nobody is at their best, everyone knows it, and carried grievances are heavy.

failureModes.symptom: Repeated arguments over small things
failureModes.cause: Exhaustion, hunger and unclear roles
failureModes.remedy: Address the physical cause first, then write the rota down.

failureModes.symptom: One person doing everything and resenting it
failureModes.cause: Competence drift — the capable person absorbs every task
failureModes.remedy: Assign deliberately, including the jobs that person does best. Rotate anyway.

failureModes.symptom: A child becoming disruptive
failureModes.cause: Fear expressed the only way available, and nothing to do
failureModes.remedy: Give them a real job and tell them the truth at their level.

doesNotDo: This does not address abuse, coercive control or violence in a household, which are emergencies of their own and need outside help, not negotiation.
It does not treat anxiety, depression, trauma or any mental health condition. Those need professional care.
It does not make a group with real pre-existing fractures cohere. Stress reveals those; it does not create them.
It does not cover decision-making in groups of strangers, which has different dynamics.

title: Children in an emergency
summary: Children take their reading of how dangerous things are almost entirely from the adults around them. That is a heavy responsibility and also the most useful lever you have.

steps.text: Tell them the truth, at their level, and say what is being done about it. Children handle honest bad news considerably better than they handle an obviously worried adult saying everything is fine.
Keep whatever routine you can. Meals at the usual times, bedtime at the usual time, the usual story. Routine is how a child measures whether the world is still working.
Give them a real job: filling bottles, counting tins, looking after a younger sibling, keeping the torch. Usefulness is the most effective thing you can offer an anxious child.
Limit exposure to repeating coverage. Young children in particular can understand a looping clip as the event happening again each time.
Expect regression — bedwetting, clinginess, thumb-sucking, tantrums, sleeping badly. It is a normal response to an abnormal situation and usually resolves as things stabilise.

Keep them physically close in the chaotic parts, and make sure each child knows the rally points, the out-of-area contact's name and number, and what to do if separated. Put that on a card in their pocket.
steps.caution: Write the out-of-area contact's number on a card for each child. A child who knows one phone number can be reunited; a child who only knows 'Mum's mobile' often cannot.

steps.text: Answer the same question as many times as it is asked. Repetition is how children process, not inattention.
Look after yourself in front of them. Your composure is the single biggest input to theirs, and taking a moment out of sight to fall apart is a legitimate tactic.

failureModes.symptom: Child increasingly distressed despite reassurance
failureModes.cause: Reassurance that contradicts what they can see
failureModes.remedy: Honest, simple information plus a concrete plan does more than reassurance.

failureModes.symptom: Behaviour deteriorating over days
failureModes.cause: Routine gone, no role, too much exposure to coverage
failureModes.remedy: Restore what routine you can, give them a job, turn the coverage off.

failureModes.symptom: Child cannot be reunited quickly after separation
failureModes.cause: They know faces, not numbers
failureModes.remedy: A card in the pocket with the out-of-area contact's name and number.

doesNotDo: This does not address trauma requiring professional care. Persistent distress, nightmares or behaviour change lasting weeks needs a clinician.
It does not cover children with additional needs, for whom disruption of routine may be far harder and needs individual planning.
It does not substitute for the school and childcare plan, which is a separate and practical piece of the household plan.
It does not cover separation or loss, which need support beyond anything a preparedness library can offer.

title: Not being the interesting one in the room
summary: The least useful thing you can do with preparation is advertise it. This is about avoidance and ordinary discretion — dress, routine, what you say and what you post — and it is explicitly not about confrontation or about evading anybody's lawful authority.

steps.text: Do not advertise what you have. The most common way a household becomes a target is telling people, cheerfully and in advance, exactly what is in the garage.

Dress for the context you are in. Clothing that matches the people around you is unremarkable; tactical-looking kit in an ordinary neighbourhood is memorable, and memorable is the opposite of what you want.
Keep your routine unremarkable rather than rigidly identical. Varying times and routes slightly is ordinary prudence; it is not evasion and should not look like it.
Manage the digital footprint. Photographs of your stores, check-ins at your home, and public posts about being away all aggregate into something useful to someone else. Review what is public.
Keep purchases and deliveries low-key. A pallet on the driveway is a public announcement.
Teach children what not to volunteer — not secrecy, which is a burden, but the ordinary difference between family business and conversation.

Be generous anyway. A neighbour who knows you and likes you is worth far more in a bad week than one who does not know you exist, and discretion is not the same as isolation. The best security a street has is the people on it.
steps.caution: Discretion is not hostility toward neighbours, authorities or responders. Cooperating with emergency services, following lawful instruction and helping the people around you are all straightforwardly in your interest.

steps.text: Decide in advance what you would share and with whom. Deciding generously, ahead of time, is far better than deciding under pressure at the door.

failureModes.symptom: Neighbours arrive expecting supplies
failureModes.cause: Told them in detail during a calm period
failureModes.remedy: Discretion beforehand, and a decision made in advance about what you would share.

failureModes.symptom: Home targeted while away
failureModes.cause: Public posts about being away, and visible deliveries
failureModes.remedy: Post after you return, and keep deliveries discreet.

failureModes.symptom: Isolation and no help when it is genuinely needed
failureModes.cause: Discretion taken as far as secrecy from everyone
failureModes.remedy: Know your neighbours. Discretion about stores, openness about yourself.

doesNotDo: This is NOT about evading, misleading or confronting law enforcement, emergency services or any lawful authority. Cooperate with responders — it is both right and in your interest.
It does not cover tactics, confrontation, weapons or defence of property, all of which are outside this library's scope entirely.
It does not mean isolating from your neighbours. A street where people know each other is safer than one where they do not, and that effect is far larger than any amount of discretion.
It does not make you invisible, and treating it as a security system rather than ordinary prudence is a mistake.
It does not cover personal security planning for stalking, domestic abuse or targeted threat, which need specialist advice and often legal support.

title: Finding your way when GPS is wrong or gone
summary: GPS fails in more ways than people expect: no power, no signal indoors or in terrain, and — during a severe geomagnetic storm — degraded accuracy while still showing you a confident blue dot. The confident wrong answer is the dangerous one.

steps.text: Know the failure modes. A dead phone, no satellite view under canopy or between buildings, and space weather, which can degrade positioning accuracy without any warning on the screen. The device rarely tells you it is unsure.
Cross-check against the world. If the map says you are on a road and there is no road, believe the ground. Navigation errors persist because people trust the display over the window.
Learn your pace count: how many double-steps you take over a hundred metres, on the flat and loaded. It turns a guess about distance into a measurement, and it works in the dark.

Navigate by handrails and catching features. Follow something you cannot lose — a river, a ridge, a power line, a major road — and pick a feature beyond your target that tells you if you have gone too far.
Use the sun for rough direction. It rises broadly east and sets broadly west; at local noon in the northern hemisphere shadows point roughly north. Rough is enough to stop you walking in a circle.
Carry a simple baseplate compass and know two things: how to orient the map, and how to walk a bearing. That is most of practical navigation and takes an afternoon to learn.
Keep a cached offline map on the phone as well. Offline maps still show the map when the data connection is gone, even if the position fix is poor.
steps.caution: An offline map is not an offline position. Without a usable satellite fix you have a map on a screen, which is a worse paper map with a battery.

steps.text: Stop when you are unsure, before you are lost. Going back to your last certain point is almost always faster than pressing on hopefully.

failureModes.symptom: Position jumps around or sits in the wrong place
failureModes.cause: Poor satellite geometry, urban canyon, canopy, or ionospheric disturbance during a geomagnetic storm
failureModes.remedy: Cross-check against visible features and navigate by terrain until it settles.

failureModes.symptom: Walked a long way in the wrong direction confidently
failureModes.cause: Trusting the display over the ground
failureModes.remedy: Orient to reality at every stop, and use catching features so an error has a hard limit.

failureModes.symptom: Phone dead halfway
failureModes.cause: Screen on and GPS running continuously
failureModes.remedy: Paper map primary, phone for confirmation, screen off in between.

doesNotDo: This does not replace proper land navigation training, which is a real skill with a real syllabus.
A compass does not work reliably near metal, vehicles, power lines or electronics, and it does not point at true north without a declination correction.
Sun direction is rough, varies by season and latitude, and is useless under heavy overcast.
An offline map does not give you a position fix — it only means the map itself still draws.
None of this helps if you do not know roughly where you started. Note your starting point before you need it.
